Rdio Scanner

Administrator Guide

Version 8.0.0. This guide covers the Rdio Scanner server and its administration interface: installing it, meeting its requirements, configuring every feature it offers, driving its APIs, and operating it day to day. The scanner webapp and the native mobile applications are not covered here. The guide links to nothing outside itself: every cross-reference is a chapter of this guide.

1 · What Rdio Scanner is, and what this guide covers

Take the audio files a software-defined radio recorder writes, and Rdio Scanner turns them into a scanner: each call is filed against the system, site, talkgroup, and unit it came from, and served to listeners. The subject here is the server — the program you install, the flags and options that configure it, the interface you set it up through, and the APIs it answers on.

One program makes a deployment. It binds one address, holds one database, and answers on two interfaces: listeners open the main interface, and you configure the deployment through the administration interface at /admin/. Chapters that follow take up the server and that administration interface, and nothing else.

How the name is said

Rdio Scanner /ˈreɪ.di.oʊ ˈskæn.ər/ RAY-dee-oh SCAN-er

What's new since version 6.6.3

Version 7 was assembled but never published, so the jump from version 6.6.3 lands on version 7 and version 8 together. The table lists what changed since version 6.6.3 — only what changes your work — and names the chapter that operates each item. For the release-by-release record, read the project's change log.

The changes since version 6.6.3, by what they touch
AreaWhat changedChapter
The logEvery entry names the part of the server that wrote it, and the log view filters on it. Messages no longer begin with the name of the internal function that wrote them. The view gained a subsystem filter, a text search, the clickable counts strip, and auto-refresh. Retention says what it removed, and says when it could not run. Lines that only ever went to the console are in the log now.14
The databaseA new schema, and four dialects: SQLite, MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL. The first start on a version 6.6.3 database migrates it in place, announces each table, and copies what it cannot carry into the migration archive instead of throwing it away.7, 24
The administration interfaceRebuilt. Sections are edited as a working copy and written with the save bar; the conflict banner appears when another session saved the same section; the systems-and-talkgroups dialog scopes a credential; the OpenAPI section reads the contract the server publishes; the Tools section exports and imports the configuration, and imports a talkgroup or unit list per system.8, 15
Talkgroups, groups, and tagsA talkgroup belongs to many groups, which is why the tag toggle is gone. System and talkgroup types name the radio standard, and the AFS systems option is gone, replaced by the Provoice type. Alert tones and LED colours are set at group, tag, system, and talkgroup level, with the group winning. Calls are delayed per system and per talkgroup.11, 12
Duplicate detectionDetection is built on the new schema, and the window is fixed: a second call landing on one system, talkgroup, and site within the fixed window counts as the first call.13
Getting audio inThe mask gained the unit label token, so a recorder that names the radio that transmitted names the unit the listener sees.10
Interfaces and APIsThe API was renewed with the older calls clients use kept working. The call history endpoints accept a listener's access code beside an administrator's session. The Model Context Protocol endpoint lets an assistant read a deployment, and write to it when it presents the administrator's credential.16, 17
The releaseThe archive carries this guide as its operating documentation, with the ffmpeg licence as plain text beside the program.4

Back up the database and the configuration file before updating. The migration carries every row across, and an old table disappears only once all of its rows have been carried or archived. The first start of the new server ends every open administrator session; expect to log in again. Chapter 24 walks the whole path.

What this guide does not cover

Listeners reach your deployment through the scanner webapp: the application on the main address, with its talkgroup list, call history, player, and live feed. A separate application, it has its own guide kept beside this one in the project's documentation, and Saubeo Solutions' native mobile applications are not covered here either. You will find no scanner webapp screen in any screenshot in these pages. When a chapter has to say what a listener sees, it says so from the server's side: the option that changes it, the credential that unlocks it, the endpoint that serves it.

One document, no loose ends

Read this guide straight through once, then consult it; it is the path from nothing to a working deployment, complete on its own terms. Operating detail for Linux, Windows, macOS, and FreeBSD sits in chapter 21; the container image with its volume and its user in chapter 4; the log's subsystems and what each reports in chapter 14; and the licence, and what it means for both interfaces the server answers, is in chapter 27. Every cross-reference is a chapter of this guide, so no page asks you to open another file.

Reading this guide offline

Stylesheet and pictures ride inside this file. Open it from an extracted release archive, a mail attachment, or a USB stick on a machine with no network: nothing external is fetched, so nothing can fail to load, and it prints with a page break at each chapter.

2 · How audio flows through the server

Two ways in, one filing step, one way out toward listeners. Learn this path and most of what you configure — and most of what goes wrong — explains itself.

In

Two paths carry a recorder's output to the server:

  • Dirwatch — point the server at a directory the recorder writes into; it reads each new audio file and takes the call's identity from the file's name, its MP3 tags, or its sidecar JSON, according to the recorder type you chose for that watch. See Getting audio in.
  • The upload endpoints — the recorder posts the audio with its metadata as form fields to POST /api/call-upload, or posts trunk-recorder's JSON sidecar to POST /api/trunk-recorder-call-upload, the older endpoint that reads the sidecar as a document, marked deprecated in chapter 10 and on its way out. A recorder using either endpoint presents an API key. See The HTTP REST API.

From either path, the ingest is the same. It resolves the system, site, talkgroup, and unit named in the metadata against your configuration: with Auto populate on, an identity the configuration does not know is created on the spot; with it off, the call is refused, and the log says why. Where the Audio conversion option asks for it, the ingest reads the audio however the recording arrived and writes it as AAC in an m4a container — small files that play in a browser — and files the call, with its audio, in the database. The server works on the audio itself, not on the file the source sent, so a recording does not have to arrive in a format a browser plays.

Audio lives in the database

Recordings are rows, not files: the server keeps them inside the database rather than beside it. The directory the server serves contains the database, the configuration file, and the server's own state. One file therefore holds the whole archive of a deployment — and that file is what you back up.

Out

  • Listeners read the recordings and the call history through the HTTP REST API and follow live calls over the server's real-time channel. Both are free to use for any purpose, under the same terms as the rest of the server, as chapter 27 states.
  • Downstreams forward calls onward to another Rdio Scanner deployment. The forward presents an API key there as well, and you scope it to the systems and talkgroups you choose.

What the server keeps

What the server holds, and where
ThingWhere it livesChanged by
Systems, sites, talkgroups, units, groups, tags, access codes, API keys, dirwatches, downstreams, optionsThe database, edited as sections in the administration interfaceYou, in a section, saved with that section's save bar
Recorded calls and their audioThe databaseThe ingest, when audio arrives
The logThe database, read in the Logs sectionThe server, as it works
Flags: addresses, database connection, TLS, servicerdio-scanner.ini in the base directory, written by -config_saveYou, in the file, or on the command line

Configuration time makes the split matter. Save a section through the running server and every open administration session is told about it; a flag, on the other hand, is read at start-up, so changing one means a restart.

3 · Requirements

One program, one database behind it. You need a machine that runs a released platform, somewhere to keep the data, and a recorder the server can read.

Platforms a release is built for

The release matrix, as the build tool defines it. Every release carries its own ffmpeg inside the program, compiled by this project's build in a container on the machine that produces the releases.
Operating systemArchitectureArchiveCarries its own ffmpeg
FreeBSDamd64rdio-scanner-freebsd-amd64-v8.0.0.zipYes
Linux386rdio-scanner-linux-386-v8.0.0.zipYes
Linuxamd64rdio-scanner-linux-amd64-v8.0.0.zipYes
Linuxarmrdio-scanner-linux-arm-v8.0.0.zipYes
Linuxarm64rdio-scanner-linux-arm64-v8.0.0.zipYes
macOSamd64rdio-scanner-macos-amd64-v8.0.0.zipYes
macOSarm64rdio-scanner-macos-arm64-v8.0.0.zipYes
Windowsamd64rdio-scanner-windows-amd64-v8.0.0.zipYes

Conversion needs no extra install: each release embeds the ffmpeg it uses inside the binary. That ffmpeg is compiled for audio: the recipe disables every component, then enables the audio demuxers, decoders, encoder, muxers and filters this server converts with, plus the pipe, fd and file protocols a recording arrives and leaves on — so no video codec, decoder, or encoder, and no network protocol, comes out of it. Every one of the eight archives carries the ffmpeg binaries this project's build compiled, in a container, from the source release its manifest pins: the FreeBSD pair against a FreeBSD sysroot, the two macOS pairs against an Apple SDK its maintainer prepares; the build host runs no FreeBSD program and no macOS program, so those three pairs are compiled and never started anywhere. Instead the build reads what they are out of the files their own link wrote, and the FFMPEG.txt beside the program names which of the two proofs an archive's binaries were proved by. A Mac is the one host that compiles a pair with its own toolchain rather than a container, and there the two macOS architectures compile each other's ffmpeg binaries, so one Apple Silicon Mac compiles both macOS archives, with Rosetta 2 letting it run the Intel programs it compiled there; go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg on that Mac compiles them, runs them, and adopts what converts. The compile is the check: the build runs the binaries it can run through the server's own conversions, asks every one of them what they register, and refuses the ones that register a video codec. Build ffmpeg by hand and the build adopts your binaries on the two macOS targets, and only when a Mac does the building: drop them in the target's bundle directory, and the run that adopts them reads and runs them. Nothing else licenses adoption — only that the file holds the machine code the target runs, and that the binaries convert.

Recorders

A recorder qualifies if it writes one audio file per transmission. How the server then reads the call's identity depends on the dirwatch type you choose, or on the fields the recorder posts.

Recorders known to work, and the paths they use
RecorderUpload APIDirwatch
Trunk RecorderYesYes
RTLSDR-AirbandNoYes
SDRTrunkNoYes
voxcallYesNo
ProScanNoYes
DSDPlus Fast LaneNoYes

Ready-made recorder configurations, in each recorder's own configuration-file form, sit in the repository under docs/examples/trunk-recorder and docs/examples/rtlsdr-airband. The worked configurations this guide walks through are in chapter 10.

Machines

The server is a single Go binary with modest appetites: a 1 GHz-class machine handles a small deployment comfortably, and a typical one runs on a Raspberry Pi 3 or newer. Budget for disk rather than CPU, because recordings pile up and your retention sets the size of the database. Seven days of a busy system is measured in gigabytes, and the Prune days option is what puts a ceiling on it.

The database deserves its own line: it is a requirement, not a detail. SQLite asks for nothing — the server writes one file into its data directory, which suits any single-instance deployment. MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL each need a database server you run plus the connection flags that name it. See The database.

If you are building from source

  • Go 1.26 or newer.
  • Node.js 20 or newer — the web applications ride inside the server binary.
  • podman, or docker where podman is absent, for the container image and for compiling the ffmpeg of every release target, since this build compiles every target's ffmpeg in a container. The build asks the machine which program it has, and takes podman when both are there.
  • A C compiler and make, on a Mac that compiles the macOS pair with the Mac's own toolchain instead of a container — either architecture for either, because the two macOS architectures compile each other's ffmpeg binaries. No container program is needed on this route, and it is the one route this build runs with the target's own toolchain.
  • The Apple SDK tree a macOS compile links against, on the machine that writes the two macOS archives: chapter 4 names where the build looks for it and what it says when the tree is missing.

There is nothing to configure in the build tool: the release matrix, the version, and the ffmpeg bundle recipe all come from the repository. The four commands in chapter 4 show what it builds, and in what order.

4 · Installation

Three paths lead to a running server: download a prebuilt binary, run the official container image, or compile from source. For the very first attempt, the prebuilt binary is the quickest look at the software; for anything you plan to operate for long, the container is the easiest to maintain, because upgrading it means pulling a new image rather than swapping files by hand.

Before choosing, settle one question: where will audio be imported? The build carries the FFmpeg executables it needs, and the server reaches the same build for every importing mode, so the build that decides your choice is the one compiled for audio. If you will connect to a broadcast feed by URL, the host importing that feed needs a build with audio support; the web interface works on any host, no matter how audio arrives. A Raspberry Pi is often the cheapest machine with a tuner attached, and the server can run on it while the interface is administered from elsewhere.

OpenRC is not supported. If the host starts services with OpenRC rather than systemd, stop here and read Running as a Service before installing.

Download a prebuilt binary

The latest GitHub release carries an archive per platform, named with the pattern rdio-scanner-<platform>-v<version>.zip, where the platform part reads like linux-amd64; the release matrix in Requirements lists every published name. Pick the archive whose platform matches the machine that imports audio — for a Raspberry Pi 3 or 4, that is linux-arm, and on a modern 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS use linux-arm64. Each archive unpacks flat, and the commands below unpack one into the current directory, which then holds rdio-scanner, the guides admin-guide.html and user-guide.html, and FFMPEG.txt:

cd /opt
unzip ~/Downloads/rdio-scanner-linux-amd64-v8.0.0.zip
./rdio-scanner

The release for your platform runs immediately; there is no installer and nothing to configure first. Start it as described in First Run and return here for the upgrade habit: replacing the binary means stopping, swapping the archive, and starting again, covered in Backup and Restore.

A word on macOS builds, because they carry special machinery. Apple requires binaries fetched over the network to pass notarisation before the operating system will open them, and the downloaded binaries are not notarised, so macOS refuses to run them. They are signed ad-hoc and include entitlements for network access, which means one local command is enough to make a copy usable; the same command suits ffprobe. Apple also requires a different binary per CPU family, so the project publishes the two macOS targets separately — pick the one matching your Mac.

On every platform, what a machine can run is what its CPU family and operating system release say, read against the release matrix in Requirements. One further rule applies to every downloaded binary: the server refuses binaries that register a video codec, and Troubleshooting names the log line it writes when it refuses one.

Windows binaries are experimental. They carry the same FFmpeg executables, and the importing rules in Getting Audio In apply unchanged.

Run the container image

The project publishes an official image under the name chuot/rdio-scanner. The container's own root filesystem is read-only by design; everything the server writes must live on volumes you provide. The server writes only inside /app/data, so the example below publishes the container's port 3000 on the host's port 3000 and mounts a directory of your own at that path:

mkdir -p ~/.rdio-scanner

docker run --detach --name rdio-scanner \
    --env TZ=America/Toronto \
    --publish 3000:3000 \
    --restart always \
    --user $(id -u):$(id -g) \
    --volume ~/.rdio-scanner:/app/data \
    chuot/rdio-scanner:latest

The image needs no arguments, and nothing from outside it is required at runtime. Check the log for the opening lines described in First Run; if the server never starts, the mount points are the first thing to recheck, and Troubleshooting collects the log lines that name a bad mount.

To keep the container alongside other services on the host, describe it in a docker-compose.yml instead of repeating flags. This is the minimum viable definition:

services:
  rdio-scanner:
    image: chuot/rdio-scanner:latest
    container_name: rdio-scanner
    environment:
      - TZ=America/Toronto
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    restart: always
    user: "1000:1000"
    volumes:
      - ./data:/app/data

With the file saved in a directory of its own, start the stack:

Build from source

Reach for this path when no published build fits your hardware, when you want the current development version, or when you are changing the code. It needs the toolchain listed in Requirements, and a checkout of the project placed in a directory of its own; the build tool is written in Go, so the commands below assume you run them from inside that checkout.

FFmpeg first. The build carries its own FFmpeg toolchain, so the FFmpeg your distribution installed is not used by the server: the program the build produces travels embedded inside the server's own executable, and a pair of executables you drop into a bundle directory takes its place only where such a drop was made. Building the media layer by hand is optional but useful, because it proves the C toolchain works before anything of the server's is involved. Choose a version from the project's pinned set rather than the newest upstream release; the build fails with the error ffversion.h missing when the checkout does not carry that header. The project publishes its supported FFmpeg versions, and the source tree keeps a directory per version, named exactly FFmpeg_5.1.6, FFmpeg_6.1.2, FFmpeg_7.1.3, and FFmpeg_8.0.1; the build reports the directory names as the versions it knows, which is how to see what a given release of the project accepts. The build command takes the version argument, compiles that pinned version of FFmpeg, installs the result into the project's ffmpeg cache directory under ~/.rdio-scanner in your home directory, and records the outcome in a JSON index file at ~/.rdio-scanner/ffmpeg/index.json. If the build fails partway, delete the incomplete directory and re-run:

go run ./cmd/build client     # the web applications the server carries
go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg     # the ffmpeg of the platform you are on
go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg macos-amd64 # another target's ffmpeg, compiled in a container here
go run ./cmd/build server     # one binary, into dist/<target>/
go run ./cmd/build dist       # the release archive of this platform, into dist/
go run ./cmd/build dist --all # every release archive, into dist/
go run ./cmd/build container  # the container image, locally

The toolchain compiles the executables itself and needs nothing beyond the toolchain listed in Requirements — it never downloads or installs compilers. Cross-compiling a C program is harder than cross-compiling the Go server, so the FFmpeg build is hosted for you: the toolchain compiles them, runs them, and adopts what converts an input file successfully, and what it adopts it packs into a bundle per target platform. You may also drop ffmpeg and ffprobe in the target's bundle directory yourself, and the build adopts them for the two macOS targets, because a macOS C toolchain runs on a Mac; a drop for any other platform stays embedded in the binary and used by nothing until the server starts an importing process. The binaries it compiles for the other architecture are run on the Mac that runs them, and the host that cannot run the binaries it compiled leaves them in the target's bundle directory, waiting for that machine; in that case the JSON index records only the executables that convert, so the compile is the check for the cross-built pair.

The server itself. Compile it without arguments and it builds for the machine you compile on:

go build ./cmd/rdio-scanner

Pass target names as arguments and it cross-compiles instead, writing each result into the matching dist/<target>/ directory: dist/linux-arm64/rdio-scanner for a 64-bit ARM board such as a current Raspberry Pi OS install, dist/linux-arm/rdio-scanner for older ARM boards including Raspberry Pi 2 and 3 systems, and dist/windows-amd64/rdio-scanner.exe for Windows. A build for the musl libc family is published under the tag linux-musl-amd64; Alpine Linux and any other musl host should use it, because a binary built against glibc will not start on those systems.

What to expect from a build. The FFmpeg stage compiles C and runs its own tests, so it takes the largest share of the time, and a failure there names the compiler or a missing development header. The Go stage finishes quickly; it fails on a missing module or a syntax error, which only happens after an incomplete checkout or a local edit. The build also runs its own web tooling to produce the interface bundle, so an interrupted first build can leave that stage looking silent for a minute while it downloads its dependencies — patience, not intervention, is the fix there.

5 · First run

You can start a fresh server with no flags at all. It opens its ports, creates its database, and prints the addresses it answers on to the console. Three things still need doing before it records anything, and the administration interface shows you exactly which three.

Starting it

./rdio-scanner

Everything the server stores — database, configuration file, recorded audio — sits under one folder called its base directory. By default that is the folder holding the executable; if the executable's folder cannot be written to, the server uses a folder called Rdio Scanner created inside your home directory; and when the program is run straight from source the executable sits in a build cache that is not a deployment folder, so the server takes the folder you started it in. Point -base_dir at a folder you choose and the server uses that instead, which is what any deployment you mean to keep should do. If the chosen base directory cannot be written to, the server says why on the console and declines to start.

This is what the console prints the first time:

Both URLs share one port until you change the defaults: the listening address serves the listener interface at / and the same port serves the administration interface at /admin/. The signing secret printed in that output signs the session credentials your browser carries afterwards. The server invents it once, keeps it in the database, and uses it ever after — so replacing it invalidates every session open at that moment.

Logging in

The address to open is http://localhost:3000/admin/. The server creates exactly one administrator account at first start, and its password is rdio-scanner. Sign in with that password, then replace it at once; a banner across the interface will keep reminding you to until you do.

When a login succeeds, the endpoint hands back a token and the browser holds it for the rest of the session. Tokens are signed with the server's secret, the server remembers the five most recent tokens it has issued, and each token stays valid for seven days: logging in again retires tokens older than that window, and any session reaches its seven-day limit it ends by itself. An address that fails three login attempts finds itself locked out of further attempts for ten minutes, and every attempt, successful or not, is filed in the log under the login subsystem.

The banner that lists what is missing

After login, the first thing the interface shows is a card naming whatever your deployment still lacks. The card is derived from your current settings, so it shrinks as you make progress, and each line points at the control that clears it:

The items the banner lists on a fresh deployment
LevelItemCleared by
WarningYou are using the default admin password, please change it from the tools / admin password menu.Tools ▸ Change password
InfoNo systems defined. Define one from the Systems menu, or turn on Options ▸ Auto Populate to have them created for you.The Systems section, or the Auto populate option
InfoNo apikeys or dirwatch defined. Set at least one to allow ingesting audio files.The API Keys section or the Dirwatch section

A first configuration, in order

  1. Set a new administration password under Tools.
  2. Create a system in the Systems section. Every call the server ingests is filed under a system, and the listener starts browsing from that level.
  3. Open a door for the recorder: create an API key if the recorder posts calls to the server, or a dirwatch if it drops files into a folder the server watches. Getting audio in covers both.
  4. Keep the Logs section open while early calls arrive. Ingest entries name the system and talkgroup each call resolved to, and a rejected call is logged with its reason.

Saving works per section: each section ends in its own save bar, and pressing it writes straight through to the running process. Every other administration session open at that moment hears about the change, and the log records an entry reading the configuration changed. Only command line flags are different — those are fixed at process start, so a flag change does need the process stopped and started again.

Writing the flags to a file

Flags only take effect at start up, so once you have settled on the set you want, add -config_save to the command line: the server translates every flag into a line of rdio-scanner.ini inside the base directory and then reads that file at every future start, sparing you the repetition:

./rdio-scanner -listen ":3000" -base_dir /opt/rdio-scanner -config_save
./rdio-scanner          # reads /opt/rdio-scanner/rdio-scanner.ini

Inside, the file is ordinary INI: one key = value pair to a line. Treat it as configuration data, keep it in your backups, and put it under version control if your deployment grows complicated enough to need diffs. The next chapter lists the keys the file can hold and explains which wins when the file and the command line disagree.

6 · Command line flags and the ini file

A flag carries the address the server listens on, the database it opens, and how it serves TLS. Every flag is read a single time, when the server boots, and -config_save writes the whole set back to a file so the command line never has to be retyped.

Reading the flag table

The tables in this chapter are checked against the server's own flag definitions every time the documentation is built: if a flag is added, renamed, or retyped in the code and the table is not updated to match, the build fails. Where a flag's meaning is obvious, the table carries only the fact that matters — its type and default. Where behaviour is easy to guess wrongly, a short note follows the table.

The flags

The table below lists every flag, in the order the server documents them. The "ini setting" column names the entry that replaces the flag in the ini file; -config_save writes them all in that spelling. Types are what the flag parser expects: a bool flag is present or absent, an int or a duration needs a value, and a string list takes the value more than once.

Every flag the server accepts
FlagDefaultWhat it decides
-admin_passwordnoneHash and store this password for the administrator, and stop without starting a server. The one flag that changes the credential from the command line. See the command line client.
-base_dirthe executable's folder, else ~/Rdio Scanner, else the folder the server was started inWhere the database file, the configuration file, and the server's state are written. Must be writable.
-bcrypt_cost10The bcrypt cost the administrator credential is hashed at, 10 to 14. A cost outside that range is refused at start-up.
-configrdio-scanner.iniThe name of the configuration file, read from the base directory.
-db_connect_timeoutnoneHow long the server waits for the database to answer, as a Go duration such as 5s.
-db_filerdio-scanner.dbThe SQLite database file, in the base directory.
-db_hostlocalhostThe database host, for MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL.
-db_namenoneThe database name, for MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL.
-db_passnoneThe database password.
-db_port3306, 5432 for PostgreSQLThe database host port.
-db_sslmodenoneThe PostgreSQL SSL mode, one of the PostgreSQL names such as disable, require, verify-full.
-db_tlsnoneThe MySQL and MariaDB TLS setting: true, false, skip-verify, or a registered TLS configuration name.
-db_typesqliteThe database backend: sqlite, mariadb, mysql, or postgresql. Anything else is refused at start-up.
-db_usernoneThe database user name.
-listen:3000The address the server answers on. :3000 listens on every address; 127.0.0.1:3000 listens on one.
-mcp_serverfalseServe the Model Context Protocol endpoint. See the MCP server.
-ssl_auto_certnoneA domain name to get a Let's Encrypt certificate for, automatically. Needs ports 80 and 443 reachable.
-ssl_cert_filenoneA PEM certificate to serve TLS with.
-ssl_key_filenoneThe PEM key that matches that certificate.
-ssl_listennoneThe address TLS is served on. Without it, TLS is served on the plain listening address when a certificate is configured.
-trusted_proxiesnoneComma-separated proxy addresses, CIDR or bare, whose X-Forwarded-For the server believes. See Reverse proxies.

Three defaults deserve a look before you override anything. The listening port is 3000, which makes a bare server answer on every interface at http://HOST:3000/ — plain HTTP, no access code, until you change them; chapters 19, 20, and 9 cover the three ways to close that gap. The log level is info: the right choice to start with, and the server tells you in its own startup output when a live setting would change that, as chapter 14 explains.

Flags only the command line can carry

The next group of flags configures the listener — the name it advertises to your phone and the device name the desktop app expects — plus the flags that write or validate the ini file itself. None of these are stored in the ini file or editable from the admin interface.

The modes the same command line selects
FlagDefaultWhat it does
-cmdnoneDrive a server that is already running: log in, read and write the configuration, change the credential, add and remove listener accesses. It is a client of the public administration endpoints. See the command line client.
-config_savefalseWrite the configuration file and stop.
-servicenoneRun under the operating system's service manager: install, uninstall, start, stop, restart, and run as the service's own command. See Running as a service.
-vacuumfalseClears the records a legacy migration left in problem — the units it left damaged, the migrationArchive table, and any legacy table it left standing — then compacts the sqlite database file, and stops without starting a server. It refuses to run while another server holds the deployment. See the database and upgrading and migrating.
-vacuum_dry_runfalsePrints what -vacuum would clear and drop, and which compaction it would skip, and removes nothing, drops no table, and compacts nothing. It stops without starting a server. See upgrading and migrating.
-versionfalsePrint the version and stop.

Precedence

The server decides where each setting comes from in one fixed order: command line flags first, then the ini file, then built-in defaults. A flag on the command line therefore beats the same setting in the ini file, and the ini file beats the default.

The ini file lives beside the executable and is named rdio-scanner.ini unless -config names another. The server reads it once, at startup; it writes the file back only when you use -config_save, and pressing Save in the admin interface writes the configuration to the database, not to the file. There is no watching, polling, or automatic reload of the file: a file changed while the server runs has no effect until the next start.

Because the admin interface and the ini file describe the same settings, they cannot both be authoritative at once: chapter 13 spells out what each one is authoritative for, and the answer is the admin interface.

What -config_save does to your file

The two ini-only flags in the table above behave very differently, and mixing them up loses work.

db_type = postgresql
db_host = db.internal
db_name = rdioscanner
db_user = rdio
db_pass = <the password>
db_sslmode = require
listen = :3000
ssl_auto_cert = scanner.example.org
trusted_proxies = 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8
mcp_server = true
bcrypt_cost = 12

-config_save rewrites the whole file from what the server currently holds: the [DEFAULT] section and any per-system sections keep the settings they hold, and everything else is laid out fresh in the server's own order with current values. A save rebuilds the file, so your comments and blank lines do not survive it — keep notes outside the ini, or re-add them after each save. If the target file does not exist yet, -config_save creates it.

-config_validate changes nothing. It parses the named file the way a startup parse would and reports what it finds. That makes it the safe check to run after hand-editing: validate first, restart second. Both flags stop the normal startup path — the server does not open a port or a database while it validates or saves. Use -config on its own if you just want to start the server pointing at an ini file that lives somewhere other than beside the executable.

The system sections

Beyond [DEFAULT], the ini file can carry one section per radio system, and the settings inside such a section apply only to that system: the unit selection, the talkgroup scan list, the record toggle, and the per-system audio settings from chapter 13. Section names are the system names exactly as the database holds them, and a name that does not match any known system at startup is logged as unrecognised rather than silently applied to something else.

The variables the server reads
VariableEffect
DOCKERSet by the container image. It marks the deployment as containerised: the directory-watcher section is removed from the administration navigation, because a watched directory inside a container is a container path and not yours.
TZThe timezone the server's clock uses — log timestamps, and the day boundaries pruning works against. Set it explicitly on a container; the container's default is not your timezone.
RDIO_ADMIN_PASSWORDThe password -cmd login reads, so a script can log in without putting the credential in a command line the process list shows.

Two rules about the section name keep the file predictable. Only the literal section [DEFAULT] applies settings to every system; a differently named section never does, and the server says so in its log when a section carries a name it did not expect. And a setting line inside [DEFAULT] that is not one of the server's known option names is reported the same way, because a typo there would otherwise sit unread for months.

If the server ignores an ini file at startup. An unread ini file is one of the few startup failures the server says so directly about, and the startup log names the file it tried to read and what went wrong. A permissions problem (the file cannot be read by the account running the server) is the usual cause; see chapter 22 for how to run the server as an unprivileged account whose groups reach the file.

Where to go next

The ini file is where the settings live, but the database decides what the server does with them. Chapter 7 explains what the database is, why it owns the live settings, and how Export settings in the admin interface turns it back into text.

7 · The database

A single database holds everything this server keeps: the configuration, the recorded calls, and the log. A flag picks the backend, only the server touches its schema, and the first start against an older database migrates that database in place.

Backends

The backends the server answers to
BackendNeedsFlags that name it
sqlite (default)Nothing. One file in the base directory.-db_file
mariadbA MariaDB server you run and a database with a user.-db_host, -db_port, -db_name, -db_user, -db_pass, -db_tls
mysqlA MySQL server, the same way.the same, with -db_tls
postgresqlA PostgreSQL server.the same, with -db_sslmode in place of -db_tls

A lone deployment wants SQLite: the database is then a file inside the base directory, opened with no network round trip, and a copy of that file is a whole backup. Choose MariaDB, MySQL, or PostgreSQL instead when other systems must reach the same data, when the database lives on a host of its own, or when site rules oblige you to run a database server. Unless you change it, the port is 3306 — or 5432 for PostgreSQL.

Start-up fails outright if the database cannot be reached: the server declines to boot. A connection that drops mid-run is logged under the database subsystem, and normal service resumes by itself the moment the database answers again.

What is stored

What the server keeps in the database
StoredWhat it is
Systems, sites, talkgroups, unitsThe hierarchy a listener browses, and the identities the ingest resolves a call against.
Groups, tags, talkgroup groupsThe ways a listener and an access code select talkgroups across systems.
AccessesThe listener access codes: identity, the systems and talkgroups they reach, the expiry.
API keysThe keys a recorder posts calls with, and a downstream presents, each scoped to systems and talkgroups.
DirwatchesThe directories the server watches, their recorder type, and their mask.
DownstreamsThe other deployments calls are forwarded to, with the address and the key.
CallsEvery ingested transmission: its identity, its start and duration, its metadata, and its audio, stored in the database with the row.
Call frequencies, call patches, call unitsThe per-call detail a recorder reports: the frequency the call ran on, the talkgroups a patch involved, the units that took part.
DelayedThe calls the downstream delivery is holding before sending them.
LogsThe server's own log, read in the Logs section.
OptionsThe options, the signing secret, and the administrator credential's hash.
Migration archiveThe rows a migration read and could not carry, with the reason. See Upgrading and migrating.

Do not look for audio files on disk. The recordings live as rows, the base directory holding nothing but the database and the configuration file, with each call's audio travelling inside the database beside its row. One file therefore backs up the deployment, and the database only ever grows as fast as your retention lets it.

Retention

A scheduled pass deletes calls older than the Prune days option, then the log entries behind them, and files the totals under the prune subsystem as retention pass removed 1 234 calls and 5 678 log entries. Give the option the value 0 and the pass is off: the deployment hoards every call and entry it has ever taken in.

The schedule belongs to the server and runs against the server's clock, which makes the host's timezone matter wherever the day boundary carries meaning. Pruning undoes what a backup preserves, so settle on your backup arrangement before choosing any retention.

When an older database is opened

Point this server at a database an older one wrote and it migrates that database as it starts: the schema moves forward, groups and tags the legacy server stored as option entries become rows of their own, and the log table is reconstructed. Where a row cannot survive the move it is written to the migration archive, naming the table and row it came from, why it was archived, and when — the server never discards anything quietly.

Each start re-runs the migration, and a row already archived simply archives as nothing rather than clashing, so a migration interrupted halfway resumes on its own. For a version 5 deployment, Chapter 24 gives the route in and the checks to make once the migration reports itself done, including what the one-shot -vacuum run clears from a migrated database: the archive, the units the migration left damaged, and the legacy tables a row the migration could not read kept standing.

Keeping it healthy

  • Back up the database file while the server is not writing to it, or take the backup from the database server's own tools. See Backup and restore.
  • Give the server-side backends a database user with the narrowest grant that lets the server work: the database, its tables, and nothing else.
  • Watch the database subsystem in the log. Connection failures, statements that failed, and the migration's own lines are filed there.
  • Do not edit the tables by hand. The administration interface is the path the server expects, and a hand-edited row is a row the server will read as its own.

8 · The administration interface

Every setting a deployment has is configured at /admin/. The server itself serves that one page, the page changes the configuration by asking the live server rather than editing anything on disk, and while you work it keeps showing what the server is doing.

Logging in, and what a session is

Login posts the password, and the server replies with a session token that the browser keeps for the rest of the visit; the interface attaches it to every request it makes. The token is signed by the server's secret and stays alive for seven days. The server remembers only the five most recently issued tokens, so signing in a sixth time retires the oldest of them, seven-day-old tokens stop being accepted, and a server that rotates its secret invalidates every session signed before the rotation.

A ten-minute lockout follows three failed logins from one address. The refusal never reveals the number of tries remaining: it reads exactly like a plain wrong password. The server records the lockout in its own log with the words too many login attempts from before the address. Behind a reverse proxy the server sees the proxy's address unless the proxy is on the trusted list — see Reverse proxies.

The navigation

The section list runs in the order of a working deployment: Dashboard first, then Systems with the Sites, Talkgroups, and Units filed under it, then Groups and Tags, then Dirwatch and Downstreams, then Access, then Options, then Logs, then Tools, and OpenAPI at the end, since that one is reference rather than configuration. Sections answering one question are placed side by side, so the neighbour of the thing you are hunting is usually where you already stand. Widen the thinking to a narrow viewport and the navigation moves above the content: the sections wrap onto several rows, each item showing its icon and its label.

The sections, and what each one configures
SectionWhat it carriesChapter
DashboardWhat the server is doing right now: how long it has been up, the listener connections it is holding, the directory watchers it started, the calls it recorded in the last 24 hours and the talkgroups busiest among them, and the errors and warnings its own log holds. It reads and never writes, and it is the section you land on after signing in.8
SystemsThe systems: each row's own fields, and the system's list of blacklisted talkgroup references.11
SitesThe sites of the system you have selected.11
TalkgroupsThe talkgroups of the system you have selected.11
UnitsThe units of the system you have selected.11
GroupsGroups of talkgroups, the way a listener selects many talkgroups at once.12
TagsTags, the labels a listener filters by.12
DirwatchThe directories the server watches for a recorder's files. Removed from the navigation when the server's environment names the container.10
DownstreamsThe other deployments calls are forwarded to.10
API KeysThe keys a recorder posts calls with, and a downstream presents.9
AccessListener access codes: who may listen, to which systems and talkgroups, until when.9
OptionsThe server's behaviour options.13
LogsThe server's own log, filtered and paged.14
ToolsExport and import the configuration, import talkgroups and units from CSV, change the password.15
OpenAPIEvery endpoint the server answers, read from the contract the server publishes.16

The system currently picked in Systems owns the sections Sites, Talkgroups, and Units: each of the three wears that system's name at its head, and every row inside belongs to it.

Dashboard opens the moment your session begins, and it is the only read-only section: its cards carry no fields, and it has no save control. Uptime and the base it runs from, listener connections held open, watchers started, the calls recorded over the past 24 hours together with the busiest talkgroups among them, and any errors or warnings sitting in its log — all of it appears as cards, and a caption under the cards gives the moment of the snapshot. The page re-reads on a five-second cycle; turn Auto-refresh off to stop that, and Read again takes one fresh reading whenever you press it. If the server falls silent, the dashboard removes its figures instead of leaving stale ones on screen and states the problem in text.

Rows, the save bar, and the conflict banner

A section is a list of rows, and every row collapses: shut, it names itself; open, it shows its fields. Systems, Sites, and Talkgroups take one open row at a time; so do Units, Access, and API Keys; and the same holds for Dirwatch, Downstreams, Groups, and Tags — opening another shuts the first, and creating a row leaves the new one open, so long lists stay manageable and the save bar never drifts away. Only the Tools panels and the OpenAPI endpoint list allow several rows open at once. The section's add control creates a row; the button on the row deletes one. Typing writes nothing.

Writing happens when the save bar does. The bar becomes enabled once the section holds valid unsaved changes, and its label names what is still unwritten. Save posts the section exactly as it stands to the live server; Discard drops your edits and replaces the form with what the server holds.

The conflict banner exists for the moment two sessions edit one section. If somebody else saved that section while your edits were open, the banner rises over the list offering Reload from server and Discard: reload brings in their version so your change can be re-applied over it, and throwing your own edits away ends the collision when your change no longer matters. Without the banner, a save would trample the other administrator's work.

A save writes through the live server, and that server then pushes the new state to every other signed-in session over a connection the interface keeps open for precisely that news; the configuration changed appears in the log. Nothing restarts — the sections take effect as they stand. The flags are the exception: they are read only at start-up, as the flags chapter explains.

The systems-and-talkgroups dialog

Systems and talkgroups bound what an access code or an API key may do, and Downstreams use the very same scoping for the audio they forward. Wherever you choose a scope — in any of those three sections — the identical dialog opens: the systems with their talkgroups beneath them, a control on each system and each talkgroup, and the groups and tags shown wherever they come into play.

What the interface tells you

  • The banner at the top of the page lists what the deployment is missing, and clears itself as you clear the items. It is on the first run.
  • A snackbar confirms what just happened — a save, an export, a password change — at the bottom of the page.
  • The Logs section is the server's own account of what it did, and it is where a problem is diagnosed. It is on the log chapter.
  • The OpenAPI section is the endpoint list the server publishes, with the authentication each endpoint takes.

The container changes one thing

If the container's environment is named in the server's environment, Dirwatch drops out of the navigation. A directory watched inside a container is a container path, but the process recording those files sits outside the container, so the section would tempt you to point the server at a path it cannot see. Mount the recorder's folder into the container and watch the mount instead; the container installation shows how to set that mount up.

9 · Access codes and API keys

A deployment deals in two credentials. The access code is what a listener presents to hear the audio; the API key is what a capture box presents to deliver it. The two lists are separate, both are scoped the same way, and they are examined at different moments — the access code the moment a listener connects, the API key the moment a recording arrives.

The two credentials, and where each one is presented
CredentialWho holds itPresented atUnlocks
Access codeA listenerThe listener application's access code prompt, and the X-Access-Code header on the call history endpointsThe live feed, and the recorded calls inside its scope
API keyA recorder, a capture box, another Rdio Scanner deploymentThe key field of an upload, and the API key field of a downstream, which is the key that deployment's server acceptsThe right to post calls, inside its scope

Access codes

The list grants listeners permission to watch the server, and each of its rows carries five things: the code itself, a display name that the log and the interface show, the moment the code stops working, how many listeners may hold it open at once, and the systems and talkgroups it unlocks.

The access code row
FieldWhat it is for
CodeThe credential. Required. The field is masked; the eye button next to it reveals it so an administrator can read it out to someone over the phone.
IdentThe name the log and the interface show for this code. It is what a log entry about an expired or locked code names.
ExpirationA date and time. Leave it empty and the code never expires. Once the moment has passed, the code is refused and the listener is told its access has expired.
LimitHow many listeners may hold this code at the same time. 0 or empty means no cap. A listener arriving at the cap is refused and told so.
Choose systemsOpens the scope dialog: Everything, Groups, Tags, or the systems and talkgroups you tick.
Delete accessRemoves the row. Nothing is written until you save the section.

Open servers and restricted ones

What kind of Rdio Scanner server you run is decided by the Access list itself. An empty access list is an open server: the server hands every listener the whole configuration and never asks for a code. Put a single entry in the list and the server is restricted: from that point it sends nothing to any listener until a code is presented.

That is the entire switch, so turn it deliberately. The first access code you add converts a server anyone could listen to into one that refuses everyone — the applications that were streaming without trouble a minute ago included — until they present a code.

What the listener is told

The server tests a code through a fixed sequence of checks, and the outcome is visible to the listener, so learn the sequence before somebody telephones you about it.

The listener's outcomes, in the order the server checks them
OutcomeWhat the listener seesWhat the log files
Attempts spentThe code prompt again, and nothing else is examined — a correct code arriving after the attempts are spent is refusedNothing: the attempts are counted, not recorded
Code not on the listThe code prompt againa listener from the address presented an access code that is not valid, once per window, not once per guess
Valid code on the last allowed attemptThe code prompt, and the code is refusedthe access code for ident … is locked after too many attempts
Expired codeThe access has expiredthe access code for ident … has expired
Limit reachedThe connection limit is reachedident … is already at its limit of N listeners, and the connection was refused
AcceptedThe live feed starts, with the configuration the scope allowsNothing. A listener joining is a Live feed entry, not a login entry

Five attempts is the ceiling, and the server keeps that count in two places: once against the session, once against the address it came from. A code that is accepted zeroes both counters. A code that is refused zeroes neither, whatever the reason for the refusal — which is why the ceiling limits trying rather than being wrong.

Because a code is a credential, the server never prints one in its log. The entry raised for a refused code names the address it came from; the entries for an expired or a locked code name the ident. The code appears in neither. And because a guessing tool must not be able to fill the log view, the warning for an invalid code is said once per window, not once per guess.

API keys

An ingest source delivers its calls with an API key. The row for a key holds the key itself, a name, a switch that turns the key off without deleting it, and the systems and talkgroups the key may upload to.

The API key row
FieldWhat it is for
DisabledTurns the key off. A disabled key uploads nothing, and the row stays where it is so you can turn it back on.
KeyThe credential. Required. The copy button next to it puts it on the clipboard, which is what you paste into the recorder's configuration.
IdentThe name for this key.
Choose systemsOpens the same scope dialog an access code uses.
Delete API keyRemoves the row.

A key created with the section's add control arrives scoped to Everything. A key with an empty scope uploads nothing, so a key you scoped to systems and then unticked everything beneath is a key that has stopped working: its uploads are refused, and the log says the key is not valid.

The path an ingest takes decides where the key rides along. A watched directory carries no key at all — the directory is the credential, which is precisely why protecting watched directories is your job. A call posted to /api/call-upload sends the key in the multipart request's key form field, and a trunk-recorder upload sends it in the very same field. A downstream row carries the key that the other server accepts, in its API key field.

A refused upload is answered 401 with the plain text Invalid API key for system <nil> talkgroup <nil>., and the refusal is filed in the log as the apikey is not valid. The recorder receives the same text it has always received; you gain a record of a box that reached the server and was turned away.

The scope dialog

The server scopes access codes, API keys, and downstreams against the same two things — a system and a talkgroup — so all three open one dialog.

  • Everything covers the whole deployment: every system, every talkgroup, and every one that gets added afterwards.
  • Groups and Tags tick an entire group or tag in one go. The box shows a third state when the scope covers part of that group — the look of a group you ticked and then narrowed inside the Systems list.
  • Systems lists each system with its talkgroup rows beneath it. Ticking a system ticks its talkgroups; untick a single talkgroup and the rest stay ticked.
  • A row states the label its section carries. A talkgroup row and a system row also state their reference in parentheses after the label — Metro (10001), Ground (1514000) — and that parenthesised number is exactly what the row's Id field holds in the Talkgroups and Systems sections. Groups and tags are named by their labels alone, since no reference number for a group or tag is shown to you anywhere else. Where the label of a system or talkgroup is empty, the row states its number alone; where the New… control has just created the row, the row states what it is: New system, New talkgroup.

A system in the scope with no talkgroups named beneath it is not in the scope at all. That is the shape the stored scope takes, and it is the one property of the dialog that catches people out: a system whose talkgroup list is empty grants nothing. A listener holding that scope sees a live feed with nothing in it, and an upload to that system is refused.

For a downstream the scope means something else: it is not what the downstream may see, it is the calls this server forwards to it. Scope a downstream to two systems and it receives those two systems' calls and nothing more; leave it unscoped and it receives nothing.

The dialog itself is photographed, with the groups and tags named, on the administration interface chapter.

A scope is a grant rather than a filter. A listener whose scope covers a talkgroup can hear it; a listener whose scope does not, cannot — and there is no setting on the listener's side of the connection that changes the arrangement. So when someone reports a talkgroup they cannot hear, the answer sits inside that listener's scope, and you start at the summary line under Choose systems: all systems and talkgroups or some.

10 · Getting audio in

There are three ways for calls to reach the server. It can watch a directory the recorder writes into; a recorder can post a finished call to an upload endpoint; or a second Rdio Scanner deployment can forward its calls downstream to this one. Most deployments pick one of the first two, and which one suits depends on where the recorder sits in relation to the server.

The three ingest paths, and when each one is the right one
PathNeedsUse it when
DirwatchA directory both the recorder and the server can reach, and the server's own file accessThe recorder writes on the same machine, or on a share the server can read
Upload endpointAn API key, and a recorder that can post to the server's addressThe recorder is on another host, another site, or behind a box you cannot mount
DownstreamThe other deployment's address and an API key valid thereTwo deployments, and one of them should carry the other's calls

Dirwatch

The server watches a folder, and the watch comes with instructions for reading whatever appears inside it: that combination is what this chapter calls a dirwatch. Every row names the recorder that writes there, and it has to, because it is the recorder that fixes where a call's descriptive data lives — in the file name, in the path, in the MP3 tags, or in a sidecar JSON file beside the recording.

The dirwatch row
FieldWhat it is for
DirectoryThe directory to watch. The recorder's own output directory: Record, 1R-Record, or VC-Record for DSDPlus Fast Lane, Recordings for SDRTrunk, captureDir for Trunk Recorder, and any directory you point a recorder at for the default type.
TypeHow a file's metadata is read. See the table below.
ExtensionThe audio extension to watch, without the period: mp3, wav.
System, Site, TalkgroupSend everything in this directory to a fixed system, site, and talkgroup, whatever the file says. Leave them empty and the metadata read from the file decides.
MaskFor the default type: the pattern that reads the metadata out of the file name. See the tokens below.
FrequencyA fake frequency in hertz shown on the listener's screen, for a recorder that reports none.
DelayMilliseconds a file is allowed to settle before the server reads it, for a recorder that writes the sidecar after the audio. The default is 2000. A delay longer than a day is clamped to a day.
Delete afterDelete the files once the call is built, so the watched directory does not fill up. On by default.
DisabledStops watching this directory without deleting the row.

The directory has to live on the server's own disk. Dirwatch does not work over networked storage: a watch laid on a network mount loses files, catches files before the recorder has finished writing them, and reports faults you have no way to put right from the server side. Direct the recorder's output onto local disk, and when the server runs in a container, point the watch at the mount rather than at the recorder's own path.

The four recorder types

What each type reads a call's metadata from
TypeMetadata comes fromWhat you set
DefaultThe file name, read with a mask you writeMask, extension, and the system, site, and talkgroup overrides
DSDPlus Fast LaneThe file path: the folder names under the record directory name the system, talkgroup, and unitThe directory, and nothing else
SDRTrunkThe MP3 tags SDRTrunk writes from its aliases tabThe directory and the extension
Trunk RecorderThe JSON sidecar Trunk Recorder writes beside the audio fileThe directory, and the extension

The mask tokens

To build a mask, take a real file name and swap the parts you want read for tokens. The server turns each token into a pattern, matches file names against the result, and hands the captured pieces to the values the tokens name. Pieces come out of the name in the order their tokens sit in the mask — no other rule decides it.

Every mask token
TokenReads
#DATEThe date: 20201231, 2020-12-31, 2020_12_31
#TIMEThe local time: 085343, 08-34-39, 08:34:39
#ZTIMEThe same shape of time, read as the call's instant in the server's zone
#SYSThe system identifier, decimal, as the recorder numbers it
#SYSLBLThe system label
#SITEThe site identifier
#SITELBLThe site label
#TGThe talkgroup identifier, decimal
#TGLBLThe talkgroup label
#TGAFSThe talkgroup identifier in agency-fleet-subfleet form, 11-061
#GROUPThe group label
#TAGThe tag label
#UNITThe unit identifier
#UNITLBLThe unit label
#HZA frequency in hertz, 119100000
#KHZA frequency in kilohertz, 119100
#MHZA frequency in megahertz, 119.100
#TGHZA frequency in hertz, and the talkgroup identifier set from it: 119100000 becomes talkgroup 119100
#TGKHZA frequency in kilohertz, and the talkgroup identifier set from it: 119100.000 becomes talkgroup 119100
#TGMHZA frequency in megahertz, and the talkgroup identifier set from it: 119.100000 becomes talkgroup 119100

For a conventional recorder that identifies its talkgroup by frequency, the mask comes out as cymx_#TG_#DATE_#TIME_#HZ; for the airband recorder worked below, as laurentides_#DATE_#TIME_#TGHZ.

Two details follow from masks being compiled as regular expressions. The first is reassuring: a mask that is not a valid expression is refused when the section is saved, so a stray bracket never makes it to the watcher. The second is a diagnostic to recognise: when the watch starts, a mask whose groups do not line up with the tokens it names is reported, with the watcher saying it captures more pieces than the mask names. That report is the shape a call with the wrong values in it takes, so do not ignore it.

Uploading a call

Either of two endpoints accepts a call as a multipart form. Both reply in plain text, and the reply depends only on the credentials, not on what the server then decides to make of the call: an accepted call is answered Call imported successfully., and credentials that are refused are answered 401 with Invalid API key for system <nil> talkgroup <nil>.

The upload endpoints
EndpointWhat it takesUse it for
POST /api/call-uploadA multipart body: the credential in the key field, the recording in the audio field, and the metadata in the fields belowA recorder, a script, or an integration that names the call's fields itself
POST /api/trunk-recorder-call-uploadA multipart body: key, the recording in audio, and Trunk Recorder's JSON sidecar in metaDeprecated. Trunk Recorder on a host the server cannot watch, until it posts to the endpoint above

Deprecated: the trunk-recorder endpoint gives way to /api/call-upload, and a future release will remove it. Trunk Recorder puts a JSON sidecar next to each recording, and only that endpoint knows how to read the sidecar as a document, which is the whole reason it exists. The general endpoint takes form fields instead, and the call it receives is the same call: to move a recorder across, read the sidecar and post its contents — system, talkgroup, frequency, site, timestamp, audio, and the rest — each under its own field name, beside the key. Beware the one silent trap: a meta part posted to the general endpoint is not read as a sidecar — it lands as an ordinary extra form field, and the call arrives stripped of everything the sidecar held.

Draw up the plan while the old endpoint is still answering, and make sure it is not some recorder nobody runs any more that discovers, one day, that the endpoint is gone.

The fields /api/call-upload reads
FieldMeaning
keyThe API key. The upload is refused when it is missing, disabled, or scoped away from the call.
audioThe recording, as a file part. Its name and content type are taken from the part.
audioFilename, audioNameThe name to file the recording under, and the type its extension implies
audioMime, audioTypeThe recording's content type
audioLengthThe recorder's own length in seconds. The server takes its word and measures nothing.
timestampThe call's instant, RFC 3339
dateTimeThe same instant under its pre-v7 name, as a Unix second count or an RFC 3339 string
system, site, talkgroupThe identifiers, as the recorder numbers them. These are matched against the identifiers your configuration uses.
systemLabel, talkgroupLabel, talkgroupNameThe labels, used to find the system and talkgroup when no identifier matched, and to name a talkgroup auto populate creates
talkgroupGroup, talkgroupGroupsThe group labels for a talkgroup auto populate creates
talkgroupTagThe tag label for a talkgroup auto populate creates
frequency, frequenciesOne frequency, or a JSON list of them with freq, dbm, pos, errorCount, and spikeCount
source, unitsThe unit identifier, or a JSON list of units with their offsets
patches, patched_talkgroupsThe talkgroup identifiers patched into this call
channelTypetrunked or conventional. Shown on the live frame for a call happening now; nothing else acts on it.

Each field is read on its own and none is required, so an unrecognised field simply reads as nothing while the remainder of the upload still lands. Placement failures pass silently: a call with no matching system, no matching talkgroup, or auto populate switched off is still answered as accepted, with the reason filed in the log under Call ingest. When the capture box claims the upload worked and the call is nowhere to be found, Call ingest is where the explanation sits.

Trunk Recorder on another host

Trunk Recorder offers an uploadScript property: after each call finishes, the recorder runs the script you name, passing the system identifier as the first argument and the recording's full path as the second. The repository carries a script that posts the recording and its sidecar to the trunk-recorder-call-upload endpoint and removes both afterwards. 

#!/bin/bash
#
# Use this script with Trunk Recorder's uploadScript system property in its
# config.json file:
#
#   {
#     ...
#     "uploadScript": "upload-call.sh 7537"
#     ...
#   }
#
# The first argument is the Rdio Scanner system identifier; Trunk Recorder adds
# the full path of the audio file as the second argument.

# The API key configured in your Rdio Scanner instance.
apikey=b29eb8b9-9bcd-4e6e-bb4f-d244ada12736

basename="${2%.*}"

curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/trunk-recorder-call-upload \
     -F "key=${apikey}" \
     -F "audio=@${basename}.wav;type=audio/wav" \
     -F "meta=@${basename}.json;type=application/json" \
     -F "system=${1:-0}"

# The audio file and its JSON sidecar are then deleted.
rm -f ${basename}.*

Replace the key and the address with your own, and hand Trunk Recorder the identifier of your system. If the recorder shares a host with the server, skip all of this and watch the capture directory: a dirwatch asks for no key, no script, and no network.

The script above posts to the deprecated endpoint; /api/call-upload is the one to use. The very same call travels to it as form fields, each named for what the sidecar called it: 

curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/call-upload \
     -F "key=${apikey}" \
     -F "audio=@${basename}.wav;type=audio/wav" \
     -F "system=${1:-0}" \
     -F "talkgroup=${talkgroup}" \
     -F "frequency=${frequency}" \
     -F "site=${site}" \
     -F "timestamp=${timestamp}"

No translation of the call is involved, because the names the sidecar uses already match the field names listed above. The full set of fields the general endpoint reads is in the table above that table, and either endpoint answers with the same two lines.

RTLSDR-Airband

RTLSDR-Airband writes one file per transmission into a folder, building each name from your template and appending the frequency while include_freq is on. A mask reads those names for the server, so the setup amounts to a recorder configuration plus a dirwatch row. 

devices: (
  {
    type = "rtlsdr";
    serial = "00000081";
    gain = 22.9;
    centerfreq = 119.1;
    channels: (
      {
        freq = 119.1;
        lowpass = 2500;
        highpass = 250;
        modulation = "am";
        outputs: (
          {
            type = "file";
            directory = "/tmp/recorders/Laurentides";
            filename_template = "laurentides";
            split_on_transmission = true;
            include_freq = true;
          }
        );
      }
    );
  }
);

Here is the dirwatch row that reads those files:

The dirwatch row for the airband recorder above
FieldValue
Directory/tmp/recorders/Laurentides
Extensionmp3
TypeDefault
SystemThe system the channels belong to
Masklaurentides_#DATE_#TIME_#TGHZ

The token that carries the whole arrangement is #TGHZ: it lifts the frequency out of the file name and makes it the talkgroup identifier, so every frequency RTLSDR-Airband records turns into a talkgroup of its own, with no channel listed by hand.

Downstreams

A downstream is a second Rdio Scanner deployment that this one re-posts its calls to. Each row holds an address to post to, the API key that deployment accepts, a switch, and the scope of the calls to forward.

The downstream row
FieldWhat it is for
URLThe other deployment's address. Only http and https are accepted, and the row is refused at save with any other scheme: the server posts your recordings and the key to this address, so it will not post them over something else.
API keyThe key the other server has in its API Keys section. A key from this server means nothing there.
DisabledStops forwarding without deleting the row.
Choose systemsThe calls to forward. A downstream with no scope forwards nothing.

Delivery to a downstream is logged as the delivery it is. The Downstreams subsystem records the system, the talkgroup, the destination, and how it went, so a call captured here that never surfaced there is explained by that entry. Three causes account for almost all of them: a key disabled at the far end, a scope that does not cover the talkgroup, and an address that fails to answer.

Auto populate

A deployment that receives calls it has no configuration for keeps working because of auto populate, which exists in two places that do different jobs: a server-wide option and a per-system switch.

What auto populate creates, and which switch decides
CreatedEnabled byNamed from
A systemThe server-wide option onlyThe identifiers and label the call claims
A talkgroupThe server-wide option, or that system's own switchThe identifiers and labels the call claims; a talkgroup with no labels joins the group Unknown and the tag Untagged
UnitsThe server-wide option, or that system's own switchThe unit identifiers the call names

Auto populate creates configuration as calls arrive — for a system, for a talkgroup, and for groups and tags when they match by frequency and the server has no row for them already. For a talkgroup, it also builds the group or tag around it on the spot. Every new row is a Configuration log entry that names the recording which caused it, so a system that appeared by itself can be followed back to the file that named it.

The counterweight is the system's Blacklists field: a comma-separated list of talkgroup references whose calls that system refuses. Blacklisting is independent of auto populate and needs no part of it enabled — once a call's system and talkgroup resolve, the refusal follows if the talkgroup's reference is in the list. A talkgroup the operator configured is therefore refused outright; one auto populate invents sails through on the very call that creates it, because the list cannot have held that reference yet, and meets the refusal from the next call onward.

You edit the list where the talkgroup is: the Talkgroups section has a Blacklist talkgroup button that appends the talkgroup's reference to its system's list and removes the row. The click stores the remaining rows together with the list, and the Systems section afterwards shows the entry. A section containing a talkgroup row the page refuses to save is rejected as a whole, naming the fields to fix. Saving a system writes the list the server currently holds, so a system saved after one of its talkgroups was blacklisted keeps that entry; a list you had been typing into the Systems section's own Blacklists field but had not saved is replaced by what the click stores, and the click says so.

A deployment that grows with the system it follows is well served by auto populate as a default; on a deployment with a fixed list it is a liability, because a capture box with a broken configuration will fill your database with talkgroups nobody named. That deployment wants the per-system switch instead.

Between them, the dirwatch, the upload endpoints, and the downstream rows are the whole of ingest, and the listener hears only what those paths let in. The next chapter takes up what the server builds from the calls once they are inside.

11 · Systems, sites, talkgroups, and units

Four object types carry the structure of your radio world into the database, and every call record refers back to them: the system the audio came from, the site it was heard at, the talkgroup the call belonged to, and the unit — the radio that transmitted. The server fills all four in as it processes audio; you fill them in, or correct them, in the admin interface's four list sections. This chapter walks the four sections, then the two questions that come up once data starts flowing: how identifiers decide which talkgroup a recording lands on, and what the colour and alert fields do.

Systems

A system is one trunked radio system, or one conventional site group you decided to treat as a unit. The fields the server tracks for it:

The system row
FieldWhat it is for
IdThe system identifier, in decimal, as your recorder numbers it. This is the identifier a recorder's metadata is matched against, and the one an access code's scope names.
LabelThe name listeners see, on the main screen and in the search panel.
TypeThe system's modulation or trunking standard: AM, DMR, FM, NFM, NXDN, P25, Provoice, SmartNet, Tetra, or no type. It is shown with the system; nothing in the server's behaviour depends on it.
Audio alertAn alert tone prefixed to every call assigned to this system. The alerts are the named oscillator sequences the server knows; they are listed in chapter 16.
Led ColorThe colour a listener's display shows for this system's calls. It wins over the talkgroup's own colour and loses to a group or a tag the talkgroup carries. Left alone, it colours nothing, and a call no level colours shows green.
Auto PopulateCreates this system's talkgroups and units when a recording names ones you have not configured. It works beside the server-wide option: see auto populate.
DelayMinutes this system's calls are held before they are propagated to listeners.
BlacklistsA comma-separated list of talkgroup references this system refuses: every call whose system and talkgroup resolve is refused when the talkgroup's reference is in the list, auto populate enabled or not. The Blacklist talkgroup action of the Talkgroups section appends a reference here and stores it with that talkgroup's rows in the click. This section saves the list the server holds: saving a system after blacklisting one of its talkgroups keeps the entry, and a list you were writing in this field and had not saved is replaced by the entry the click stores, which the click tells you.

The skip list names the talkgroups on this system you never want recorded; see chapter 12 for how skip lists are assembled. The overlay is a frequency list file. Systems appear in the Open Channels tab and as the left-hand filter on the Logs tab.

Sites

A site is one physical location within a system: a control site, a simulcast transmitter, one tower of a trunked site cluster. The server records the site on every call record, which is what lets the Logs tab filter by location. The Sites tab lists what the server has seen; add, edit, and delete the same way as systems.

Talkgroups

A talkgroup is the channel you listen to. The fields the server tracks:

The talkgroup row
FieldWhat it is for
IdThe talkgroup identifier, in decimal, as the recorder numbers it.
LabelThe label shown on the main screen and on the listener's buttons.
NameThe name shown on the main screen, beside the label.
GroupsThe groups this talkgroup belongs to, ticked in place. A talkgroup in no group is selected on its own and nowhere else.
TagThe one tag this talkgroup carries, chosen from the Tags section.
Audio alertAn alert tone prefixed to this talkgroup's calls.
Led ColorThe colour this talkgroup's calls show in a listener's display. It is the last level read, so it colours the call only when no group, tag, or system colours it. Left alone, it colours nothing, and a call no level colours shows green.
TypeThe talkgroup's channel type, shown to listeners.
FrequencyA fake frequency in hertz shown on the main screen, for a talkgroup the recorder reports no frequency for.
DelayMinutes this talkgroup's calls are held before they are propagated to listeners.
Blacklist talkgroupAppends this talkgroup's reference to its system's blacklist and removes the row from the section, so the server stops taking calls on it: the click stores the removal and the new entry in one save, and the Systems section shows the entry after it. A section holding a talkgroup row the page will not save is refused, and says which fields to fix.
