The list itself lives on the system row, where the Systems section shows it as text in its Blacklists field and saves the list the server holds; a list left unsaved in that field is replaced by this entry, and the click says so.

The alpha tag is the display name: it labels the recording on the Logs tab, the playback page, and the import and export files. The group field places the talkgroup in one of your groups, and the colour and alert fields feed the badge colours on the Logs tab — explained further down.

Units

A unit is a radio — a dispatcher console, a mobile, a portable. The unit table is mostly a name dictionary: the server learns IDs from the air and pairs them with the names it is given, which is what turns a numeric ID on the Logs tab into a readable transmitter name.

The unit row
FieldWhat it is for
IdThe unit identifier, in decimal, as the recorder names it.
Range from, Range toA range of identifiers this one row covers, so a fleet of identifiers that share a label is written as one row.
LabelThe name the listener sees for the unit.

Identifiers, and how a recording finds its talkgroup

Every object in the database is named by a numeric identifier. Two of them do most of the work in the scanner world:

  • an RFSS — radio frequency subsystem — identifies one site, which is the site in the table above;
  • an ICallID identifies one talkgroup, and a CSlot names the slot (1 or 2) on the channel where the group lives; the pair together selects the talkgroup record.

A call record carries all four identities — system, site, talkgroup, unit — as identifiers, plus the decoded text fields. That is why the list sections in this chapter matter before the Logs tab reads well: an unknown ID shows as a number until you name it.

Alerts, colours, and which one wins

A talkgroup can carry three display decorations: a colour, an alert flag, and an animated alert flag. The rules on the Logs tab are short:

  • the talkgroup's colour paints its name badge on the Calls list and the import preview;
  • a talkgroup flagged as an alert paints it in the alert colour, and an animated alert flag adds the blink — the flag pair beats the plain colour;
  • the group a talkgroup belongs to can override both: an alerting group marks its talkgroups' records with the alert colour on the Calls list, and the greylist option on a group greys its talkgroups' names out.

The four colour fields are read in one order wherever a listener's display paints a call: the group a talkgroup belongs to, then its tag, then its system, then the talkgroup itself. A level left at its default colours nothing, and a call that none of the four colours shows in green. The server works that order out before it sends a listener its configuration, so the system and talkgroup entries of that configuration arrive carrying a colour rather than an empty one for the listener to resolve: a system's entry carries the colour you chose for it, or green when you chose none, and a talkgroup's entry carries the colour that order resolves to for that talkgroup. The group and tag listings carry what you stored, and a group or tag you left alone carries no colour at all.

Importing the list

Rekeying thousands of talkgroups by hand is not the intended path. The Tools menu has an Import item that reads a spreadsheet export and replaces the whole set of systems, sites, talkgroups, groups, and units in one pass — the field names it expects are the column headers of the matching export. Keep a copy of the current export first; see chapter 23.

Next: chapter 12 builds the two collections you organize those talkgroups into: groups and tags.

12 · Groups and tags

Two collections let you organize the talkgroups you just filled in: groups are folders with behaviour — a talkgroup belongs to exactly one, and the group's settings change how its talkgroups are recorded and displayed; tags are labels with no behaviour — a talkgroup can carry as many as you like, and they exist to make searching the logs by theme possible. This chapter covers both list sections and where each one reaches into the rest of the deployment.

Groups

A group is one level of organization between a system and a talkgroup: the scanner's own call categories, a department, a shift, whatever division of your radio world you actually browse by. The fields the server tracks:

The group row
FieldWhat it is for
LabelRequired. The name shown on the listener's main screen, in the search panel, and in the select panel.
Audio alertAn alert tone prefixed to every call assigned to this group. It wins over the system's and the talkgroup's alert.
Led ColorThe colour this group's calls show. It is the first level read, so it wins over its tag's, its system's, and each talkgroup's own colour. Left alone, it colours nothing, and a call no level colours shows green.
Delete GroupRemoves the group. The talkgroups that were in it stay, and become members of no group.

The hide option removes the group and everything inside it from the web option list, so listeners cannot opt into it at all. The greylist option greys its talkgroups' names out on the Calls list; the alert flag marks the group's records with the alert colour. The order field controls where the group sorts on the Calls list.

Tags

A tag is a plain name you can attach to any talkgroup, and a talkgroup can carry any number of them. The server itself uses tags for its own categories: the radio standard the talkgroup runs on — DMR, P25, NXDN, m17 — and the modes it has seen — encrypted, clear, unknown-encryption. The tag table holds the free-form tags you add on top; the tag field on a talkgroup row lists everything attached to it.

The tag row
FieldWhat it is for
LabelRequired. The name shown on the listener's main screen and in the search panel.
Audio alertAn alert tone prefixed to every call on a talkgroup carrying this tag. It wins over the system's and the talkgroup's alert, and loses to the group's.
Led ColorThe colour calls on a talkgroup with this tag show. It wins over the system's and the talkgroup's colour and loses to a group's. Left alone, it colours nothing, and a call no level colours shows green.
Delete TagRemoves the tag. Talkgroups that carried it are left untagged.

Tags do not change recording behaviour. They are a browsing tool: the Logs tab filters by tag, and the talkgroup import and export files carry them, so a well-planned tag scheme survives a re-import.

Groups and tags in the rest of the deployment

Both collections show up beyond their own sections:

Where groups and tags are used
Used byHow
The listener's select panelA group is selected as one item, and brings its talkgroups with it.
The scope dialogGroups and Tags are the two shortcuts for writing an access code's, an API key's, or a downstream's scope: ticking a group ticks its talkgroups. See the scope dialog.
Alerts and coloursThe assignment order is group, then tag, then system, then talkgroup.
Auto populateA talkgroup created from a recording that names no group joins the group Unknown and carries the tag Untagged. A recording that names group and tag labels creates them under those names.
The logA group, tag, or talkgroup the server created because a recording named it is a Configuration entry naming the recording.

Next: chapter 13 walks the Options tab — the one section you review once per install and rarely touch again.

13 · Options

The Options tab holds the deployment-wide switches: the server's public name, the audio conversion mode, the import and export toggles, and retention. Every setting is one row of the options table, changed from this one section, and the change is live as soon as the save bar commits it — no restart. Two of these settings deserve real attention before you leave the section: the audio conversion mode, because it decides what ffmpeg does to every call that arrives, and retention, because it decides how long that decision stays undoable.

The full field list, as the form shows it:

The options, with their defaults
OptionDefaultWhat it does
Audio ConversionEnabled without normalizationConverts an ingested recording to AAC in an m4a container at 32 kbit/s with ffmpeg, so a recording in any format the recorder writes plays in a browser. See the modes below.
Auto PopulateOnGlobally allows the creation of systems, talkgroups, and units a recording names that you have not configured. The per-system switch is on a system row. See auto populate.
Branding LabelEmptyA line of text shown above the listener's main screen, to identify which instance a listener is looking at.
Disable Duplicate Call DetectionOff, so detection is onStops the server discarding a recording that duplicates the one before it: two calls on the same system, talkgroup, and site within half a second are the same call. The window is fixed at 500 milliseconds.
Email SupportEmptyThe address listeners are pointed to when they need support.
Keypad Beep StyleUnidenThe tones a listener's keypad actions synthesize: the Uniden set or the Whistler set.
Max Clients200How many listener connections the server holds at once. A listener arriving when the cap is reached has its connection closed, with nothing said on it.
Prune Days7How long the call history and the log are kept. The retention pass runs once an hour. 0 switches retention off, and a deployment with retention off writes no retention entry.
Show Listeners CountOffShows how many listeners are connected, on the main screen and in the live feed.
Sort TalkgroupsOffSorts the talkgroup lists by identifier, instead of the order you dragged them into.

Two fields on this form are not ordinary text: timezone changes how timestamps render for every listener, and import/export enabled gates the Import and Export menu items entirely — with either switched off, the menu item is gone, not merely disabled.

Audio conversion, in its four modes

Every call the server records passes through ffmpeg on its way to disk. The mode decides what ffmpeg does. The table first, the explanations under it:

The audio conversion modes
ModeWhat the server does with a recording
DisabledStores the recording exactly as it arrived and runs nothing. A recording the browser cannot play is a recording the listener cannot play.
Enabled without normalizationReads whatever audio the source sent and writes it as AAC at 32 kbit/s in an m4a container. Loudness is whatever the recorder captured.
Enabled with normalizationReads and writes the same way, and applies ffmpeg's loudness normalization to the result, with a three-second pad so a short transmission is not clipped by the filter.
Enabled with loud normalizationThe same, with the loudness target fixed: −16 LUFS integrated, −1.5 dBTP true peak, 11 LU loudness range. This is the mode for a deployment whose recordings come from recorders with wildly different gains.

Three practical notes about the modes:

  • the audio conversion step is one of the two paths through which the upload profile's Deprecated settings reach the recorded files — the server applies the conversion settings to uploaded audio the same way it applies them to its own audio sources;
  • the server never converts recordings retroactively, so switching to Original on an install that recorded MP3 leaves the old MP3 files as they are; and
  • None means the server stores exactly what the source sent, so playback depends on what your browser accepts — and the troubleshooting checklist starts by switching the mode back to MP3 if calls stop appearing.
  • a recording whose audio the converter cannot read is stored exactly as it arrived, the call is still filed, and the ffmpeg entry the ingest writes carries the reason the converter gave, at the end of it: see the log.

Retention

The retention settings decide how long recordings and call records live. There is no delete-what-you-don't-want filter yet; the settings are blunt: a maximum age in days and a maximum count of calls, and the server prunes against both, keeping whatever fits. The same settings decide what an export carries, because export works from the call records, not the files.

Disk usage is the consequence to watch. A recording is a few hundred kilobytes a minute at typical settings, and a busy system runs all day; chapter 23 covers the backup math, and chapter 25 covers what to do when the disk fills anyway.

What is not in Options

Three things people expect to find here live somewhere else: recording on or off is an Open Channels decision, per channel; the upload profile's Deprecated fields live in the Access & API keys section, as an accident of history; and the web option list — which groups and systems listeners can choose from — is derived from the hide flags on systems and groups, not set here.

Next: chapter 14 spends a full chapter on the tab you will actually live in: the Logs tab.

14 · Logs

Everything the server does leaves a line in the log, and each line names the part of the server that wrote it. When a deployment misbehaves, you never read the whole log: you ask for the directory watchers, or for the logins of the past hour, and look at nothing else.

The log is in three places, and it is the same log

  • the Logs section of the administration interface, at /admin/;
  • the console the server runs on — on a service deployment, what journalctl -u rdio-scanner shows;
  • the logs table in the database.

Three levels exist: Informative, Warning, and Error. Material that once only ever reached the console now goes into the log too, so you can search it instead of having had to be watching for it: the base folder being served, the server stopping, a fresh signing secret, and everything said about a listener connection that could not be read, understood, or written to. The single exception is the trio of notices naming the addresses the server listens on. Those stay on the console, because they tell a person where to point a browser rather than what the server did.

In storage, an entry is the event in system words, and where something failed the failure's own text comes directly after it. The console and the service log put the level and the subsystem in front of the same message, which is what lets a terminal-operated deployment see the subsystem split: 

warn dirwatch: the watcher for /data/rdio/watch/trunk stopped: no such file or directory

Grepping works off that marker: journalctl -u rdio-scanner | grep ' dirwatch: ' pulls out exactly one subsystem's lines.

The subsystems

Subsystem names form a fixed list, and the log view holds to it. Ask for a subsystem this server does not have and the request is refused outright — a bad request, not an empty result. An empty result would claim nothing happened, when in truth you asked for something this server cannot report.

Every subsystem the server files entries under, and what it reports
SubsystemShown asWhat it covers
serverServerThe server starting, the base folder it serves, and the server stopping — including an address it could not stop answering.
configConfigurationA configuration you saved, a configuration that could not be saved, and a system, talkgroup, group, tag, or unit the server created because a recording named it.
dirwatchDirectory watchersThe watched recording directories: starting a watch, losing one, reading one, and handing a recording to the ingest path.
downstreamDownstreamsSending a call to another Rdio Scanner deployment.
delayerDelayed callsCalls held back by the Delayed feature: holding one, releasing one, and failing to do either.
ingestCall ingestA recording becoming a call, and a recording that matches no system or talkgroup the server knows.
loginLoginsA refused attempt, too many attempts from one address, a sign-in or sign-out the server could not carry out. A sign-in that worked writes nothing: the administration interface's own connection records that an administrator arrived, under Administration.
accessAccess codesA client presenting an access code that is not valid, expired, locked, or already at its connection limit.
livefeedLive feedListeners joining and leaving, how many there are, and what the server could not read from or write to one.
ffmpegAudio conversionConverting a recording to playable audio. The entry carries what the converter said, and the reason is at the end of it.
uploadUploadsAn upload the server refused, and the reason it refused it — the text the recorder gets back.
pruneRetentionThe retention pass, how much it removed, and what stopped it removing anything.
logsLog searchThe log view failing to answer a search.
databaseDatabaseThe database migration: what it migrated, what it refused, and what it left damaged.
adminAdministrationThe administrator account: a password changed or not changed, a user added or removed, a new signing secret, the administration interface's own connection — joined, ended, or presenting a session token this server did not issue — and a request from the administrator whose body the server could not read.
mcpAssistant surfaceThe Model Context Protocol endpoint, when it is enabled: a caller it would not let in, named by the address the request came from; a capability refusing a caller; a capability that changed the deployment; and the endpoint's own transport trouble. It files no entry for a read an assistant was entitled to, and no entry ever carries a credential.
maintenanceMaintenanceWhat a maintenance run cleared from the deployment: the unit rows carrying their own radio number as their label, the tables the previous server left standing, and the archive that held what the migration could not carry. Each removal is one entry, and a run that cleared nothing files nothing.
callsCallsA call an operator acted on, such as pinning one. The current server writes nothing under this name; on a database upgraded from the previous server it holds the entries that server wrote.
legacyFrom the previous serverEntries that arrived before this field existed, or from a server that does not write it.

Older entries were left exactly as they were written. Each was filed under the subsystem its old line prefix implies — invalid login attempt became a login entry, dirwatch.walkdir: a dirwatch entry — and a line whose prefix matches nothing is labelled From the previous server. So a log that predates the upgrade remains readable and remains filterable.

Searching

Above the log table sit six controls and two buttons.

The log view's controls
ControlWhat it does
Sort orderOldest first or newest first. Newest first is the default, and is what you want when something just broke.
DateNarrows to one day, and the window depends on the sort order. Oldest first takes the minute you chose and runs forward a full day. Newest first runs back a day from the minute you chose and then back again by that same hour and minute, so the window is shorter than a day and usually lands on the day before the one you typed. An empty table after choosing today is normally this, not a log with nothing in it: try the other sort order, or the same date at 00:00.
LevelInformative, Warning, or Error, or all of them.
SubsystemOne of the names above, or all of them.
TextA substring of the message, matched without regard to case. A % or an _ you type matches itself.
Auto-refreshKeeps the view current, once every ten seconds, and skips a refresh while one is already in flight.
ReloadRuns the search again.
ResetClears every filter and runs the search again.

Over the table itself is a strip of counts: for everything your current filters match, how many lines each part of the server contributed, ordered from noisiest down. Each count is also a button. Press Directory watchers (137) and the subsystem filter snaps to dirwatch, leaving you those 137 entries and nothing else. The strip ignores any subsystem filter already in force — narrowing it to the single subsystem you picked would leave nothing left to click — which is also why the counts always sum to the search total on screen.

The table pages in tens; the view asks the server for two hundred at a time and keeps the rest.

Retention

Prune days sets how long the log and the call history live, and the server runs the retention pass once an hour. Put 0 in the option and retention is off — such a deployment leaves no retention entry in the log at all. When a pass does run, it reports what it removed: 

info prune: the retention pass removed 1204 calls and 318 log entries

When a pass cannot run, the entry says so, and gives the reason. Both wordings exist on purpose: a pass that announced itself before doing any work made failures indistinguishable from successes, and a pass that had quietly stopped deleting stayed invisible until the disk filled up.

Reading the log when something is wrong

Where to look, by what you are chasing
What you are chasingStart here
Recordings are not being picked upDirectory watchers, then Call ingest. A watch that started names the directory; a watch that stopped, or a directory that could not be read, names the directory and the failure; a recording that matches no talkgroup says so.
A call was recorded but never reached another instanceDownstreams — the line names the system, the talkgroup, the destination, and the outcome.
Calls are being held and not releasedDelayed calls.
Someone cannot sign in, or something is tryingLogins. Attempts, refusals, and the address they came from. A sign-in that worked writes nothing here; Administration is where the interface's connection appears.
Clients cannot listenAccess codes and Live feed.
Audio will not playAudio conversion. The entry carries what the converter said, and the reason is at the end of it.
A capture box's upload is refusedUploads. The entry names the reason the server gave, which is the text the box gets back.
The server restarted, or stoppedServer.
A system, talkgroup, or unit appeared on its ownConfiguration. Each entry names the recording that caused the server to create it, so the question becomes which recording that was.
The administration interface itself is doing something oddAdministration. The connection joining and ending, a session token this server did not issue, a new signing secret — which ends every session that was open before it — and a save whose body the server could not read.
You are not sure the history is being trimmedRetention. A pass that ran says how much it removed; a pass that could not run says what stopped it.
You are not sure the log itself is workingLog search — the log view's own failures are entries too.
An upgrade from the previous server went wrongDatabase: what it migrated, what it refused, and what it left damaged.

A text search narrows within a subsystem: pair Call ingest with a talkgroup number, Directory watchers with a directory, or Logins with an address.

15 · Tools

Tools is where a deployment moves things through files: the configuration out as a single JSON document, a configuration back in, a talkgroup or unit list arriving from another application, and the administrator password being replaced.

Export and import the configuration

Choosing Export config gives you one JSON file holding the saved configuration — every section exactly as the server has it, without the working copies of sections still open. Treat the file as the deployment's own record: keep one before an upgrade, copy one to stand up a second deployment, and attach one whenever you ask for help.

Import works the other way: a configuration JSON file lands in the sections' working copies and nothing more. The caption beneath the file picker says so outright, and the distinction is worth taking seriously. Once an import has run, every section carries unsaved changes and an enabled save bar, and the deployment itself moves only when you save the sections you mean to apply.

A whole configuration has just arrived inside a running deployment. Save the sections you reviewed and throw away the ones you did not, because the sections you never opened keep their imported working copy, and any save bar pressed later will write theirs out too. A configuration from a different deployment also brings that deployment's access codes, API keys, and downstreams along.

Import talkgroups and units from CSV

Talkgroup lists from other applications come in one system at a time: select the system, pick the CSV file, and the section first shows the rows it intends to write.

The CSV imports
ImportColumnsNotes
Import talkgroupsid, frequency, label, group, name, tag, descriptionGroups and tags the file names that the deployment does not have are created automatically. The rows are written into the system you picked.
Import unitsid, labelThe units are written into the system you picked.

That preview table puts a remove control on every row, so unwanted rows are struck out on the way in rather than deleted afterwards.

Change the password

The password panel asks for three things: the current password, a new one, and the new one a second time. Eight characters is the floor for the replacement, and nothing is written until the server has checked the current password against its own record. Get that wrong and the change is refused, with a log entry stating that the password was not changed and the reason why.

While a server is still on the password it shipped with, the todos banner at the top of the administration interface keeps saying so; change the password and the banner falls quiet. Open sessions survive the change untouched: the session token is signed with the server's signing secret, never with the password. See security hardening.

A lost password is recovered through the program rather than the interface: the -admin_password flag stores a new administrator password on the machine where the server runs, which is where the database lives. What you type becomes a command-line argument, visible to every other process on that machine, so run it where the server runs and away from any share.

16 · The HTTP REST API

HTTP traffic reaches the server from three kinds of caller: an administrator session, a listener with an access code, and an ingest source with an API key. Every action of the administration interface travels through these same endpoints, so anything a screen lets you do, a script can do as well.

The three credentials

How each credential is presented
CredentialWhere it goesWhat it opens
Administrator sessionThe Authorization header, carrying the token from the login endpoint with no Bearer prefixEvery administration endpoint: the configuration, the log, the alerts, the password, the access users
Access codeThe X-Access-Code headerThe call history endpoints only, beside an administrator session. A server with no access list answers them to an anonymous caller.
API keyThe key field of an upload's multipart bodyThe two upload endpoints

Sessions run on a token signed with the server's signing secret, valid for seven days, and the server remembers the last five tokens it handed out. Generate a new signing secret and every session opened before it stops working. Any refused request gets 401 with an empty body — at every entry point alike — so a script is never told which credential it got wrong.

The endpoint list

The OpenAPI section of the administration interface renders the endpoint list live from the contract the server publishes, in the contract's own groupings, marking the credential each endpoint accepts. The table below is that same list, annotated with what each endpoint is for.

The endpoints the server answers
Method and pathTakesWhat it does
POST /api/admin/loginnothingExchanges the administrator password for a session token, and reports that the shipped password is still in use.
POST /api/admin/logoutsessionInvalidates the token the caller presents.
GET /api/admin/configsessionThe whole configuration, under the key config.
PUT /api/admin/configsessionReplaces configuration sections from a whole-configuration body. Only the top-level keys the body names are applied.
GET /api/admin/config/{section}sessionOne section.
PUT /api/admin/config/{section}sessionReplaces one section, persists it, and broadcasts the whole configuration to the administration sessions that are open.
GET /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/sitessessionThe sites of one system.
PUT /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/sitessessionSaves the sites of one system.
GET /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/talkgroupssessionThe talkgroups of one system.
PUT /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/talkgroupssessionSaves the talkgroups of one system, and the system's blacklist with them when the body carries it.
GET /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/unitssessionThe units of one system.
PUT /api/admin/config/systems/{systemId}/unitssessionSaves the units of one system.
GET /api/admin/alertssessionThe named alert oscillator sequences the alert selects list.
POST /api/admin/logssessionSearches the log: sort order, date, level, subsystem, text, and paging.
GET /api/admin/statussessionReads what the server is doing right now: uptime, open connections, the watchers actually running, the calls waiting out a hold, the last 24 hours of calls, and the errors and warnings the log holds. The dashboard is built from this read.
POST /api/admin/passwordsessionChanges the administrator password. The current password is verified.
POST /api/admin/user-addsessionAdds a listener access code, with its ident, expiration, limit, and scope.
POST /api/admin/user-removesessionRemoves every access code sharing the user name the body names.
POST /api/calls/searchsession or access codeSearches the recorded calls, inside the caller's scope.
GET /api/calls/{callId}session or access codeOne recorded call.
GET /api/calls/{callId}/audiosession or access codeOne recording.
POST /api/call-uploadthe key fieldUploads a call as multipart form fields.
POST /api/trunk-recorder-call-uploadthe key fieldDeprecated. Uploads a trunk-recorder call: the JSON sidecar in meta, the recording in audio. A future release removes it; post the same call to /api/call-upload as form fields.
GET /nothingThe scanner webapp.
GET /adminnothingRedirects to /admin/, so the interface's relative addresses resolve inside its own subtree.
GET /admin/nothingThe administration interface.

Two connections, not requests

Two paths want a held connection instead of a single request.

  • The listener connection arrives over the address the scanner webapp is served from: one path answers both a browser and a listener, and the upgrade header settles which. Before any call streams, on a restricted deployment the server asks a restricted server's listeners for an access code and sends each one the configuration its scope grants. It matters that the connection carries no licence restriction of its own: the same GNU General Public License covers it as every other interface the server answers, as chapter 27 states, and what gates it is the deployment's own access code.
  • The administration connection lives at /api/admin/config, and it is how an open administration session finds out the configuration has moved: the server broadcasts every save to every session, which is why a conflict banner appears on a page that was already open.

What the endpoints answer

  • Administration endpoints answer in JSON, and a failure carries the status with an empty body.
  • The upload endpoints answer in plain text — the recorders posting to them read a line rather than a JSON document: Call imported successfully. once the call is taken, and Invalid API key for system <nil> talkgroup <nil>. alongside 401 when the credential fails, as the chapter on getting audio in describes.
  • Send a method an endpoint does not accept and the answer is 405; the upload endpoints reply with a line of text and file the event in the log, since a recorder posting the wrong method is a misconfiguration that will keep posting.

The writing endpoints are precisely the endpoints the interface drives, and they write into the running server: a configuration pushed through the API takes effect immediately, and is filed in the log as a configuration change. The flags sit outside this list entirely — the flags chapter is where those are set.

Reading the contract

The published contract is machine-readable, and it is what the OpenAPI section reads. Every path is named there with its method, the credential it takes, and the shape of its bodies. Reading it from a running server is the quickest way to learn what that server answers, and the endpoint table above is checked against it.

17 · The MCP server

The Model Context Protocol is a way for an assistant to work with your deployment: it reads the configuration, searches the call history and the log, and, once it has been handed the administrator's credential, edits the deployment for you. Nothing of the sort is reachable until you switch it on, and once on it sits under /mcp.

Enabling it

Start the server with -mcp_server and the endpoint comes into existence; the ini file spells the same thing as mcp_server = true. Without it the path is never registered, a request there gets the same answer as any unknown path, and the log stays quiet about the attempt.

Who reaches it, and how far

There is no third credential for this endpoint. It accepts the pair the rest of the server accepts, and whichever one arrives fixes the caller's tier.

The two tiers, and what each one may do
Credential presentedTierWhat it opens
Authorization with an administrator session tokenAdministratorRead and write: the whole endpoint
X-Access-Code with a listener access codeRead-onlyThe call history and the configuration reads, inside the scope that code carries
Nothing, on a server with no access listRead-onlyThe reads the anonymous listener is entitled to
Anything the server does not acceptrefusedAn empty 401, and the protocol handler is never reached

The administrator's credential is the one looked at first, so a leftover X-Access-Code header cannot demote someone who presented the administrator's. Rejections are filed under the Assistant surface subsystem, and what is kept is the address the request came from: the credential itself never reaches the log.

What the endpoint carries

Every capability on the endpoint is a use case the server already has, reached through the handlers the administration interface goes through. Nothing new is added for an assistant, and no tool or prompt lets one connect as a listener.

The tools
ToolReachWhat it does
list_systemsRead-only and administratorThe systems, as the configuration has them.
search_callsRead-only and administratorSearches the recorded calls, inside the caller's scope.
get_callRead-only and administratorOne call, with its recording.
diagnose_feed_problemRead-only and administratorOne pass over the calls, the log, and the configuration for a listener who hears nothing.
inspect_systemAdministratorA system with its sites, talkgroups, units, alerts, and colours.
search_logsAdministratorThe log, with the filters the log view has.
explain_errorAdministratorOne log entry, read against the configuration that produced it.
analyze_healthAdministratorThe deployment's state: the log's warnings and errors, the configuration, the retention.
manage_configAdministrator, writesReads and replaces a configuration section, and a system's sites, talkgroups, and units.
manage_access_userAdministrator, writesAdds and removes listener access codes.
rotate_admin_passwordAdministrator, writesChanges the administrator password.
The prompts
PromptWhat it asks an assistant to do
daily_health_reviewRead a day of the deployment: the log's warnings and errors, the configuration, and what changed.
explain_recent_errorsTake the recent log errors and say what they have in common.
troubleshoot_silent_talkgroupFind out why a talkgroup stopped reporting.
audit_access_codesRead the access codes: who is expiring, who is at its limit, who has no scope.
onboard_listenerWrite an access code for a listener: ident, scope, expiry.

The resources present the configuration as documents: version, systems, options, groups, tags, access codes, API keys, watched directories, downstreams, alerts, the sites, talkgroups and units of one system, and part of the log selected by level and by date. The listener-facing documents are readable on the read-only tier; the others want the administrator's.

Hand an assistant an administrator session token and it can change the deployment: create an access code, overwrite a configuration section, set a new administrator password. A token like that is worth treating as what it is — pass it only to the assistant doing the job, only for as long as the job takes, and end the session when the job is finished. Tools that write leave their mark in the log, so you can read back exactly what the assistant changed.

18 · The command line client

The same rdio-scanner you installed also drives a server that is already up. Add -cmd followed by an action and it signs in, performs that action, and exits: the administration endpoints behind the web interface, used from a shell, from a script, on a machine with no browser.

Its only requirement is network access to the server's address, so it needs neither the database nor any of the deployment's configuration, and it runs on any machine that can reach the instance you are administering.

The actions

The -cmd actions
ActionWhat it doesOptions it takes
loginSigns in and keeps the session token for the commands that follow+password, or the environment
logoutEnds the session the token file holdsnone
config-getWrites the server's configuration to a file+out <file.json>
config-setSends a configuration file to the server, applying the sections it names+in <file.json>
admin-passwordGives the server a new administrator password+password <password>
user-addAdds a listener access code+ident, +code, and the optional +expiration, +limit, +systems
user-removeRemoves every access code sharing an ident+ident <ident>
helpPrints the list above, with the examples and the defaults for your systemnone
The options every action takes
OptionWhat it names
+urlThe server to talk to. Default http://localhost:3000/. An address that is not http or https stops the client before it reads anything else.
+tokenThe session token keystore. Default is a file named for the program, in the folder the server writes its data in.
+systemsThe systems an access code is scoped to, as system identifiers: 10001,10002.
+expirationAn access code's expiry, in RFC 3339 form.
+limitAn access code's simultaneous-listener cap.

Logging in without leaving the password in the shell

The password is taken from the environment before anything else, which is why the examples in the usage text read like this: 

$ RDIO_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<password> ./rdio-scanner -cmd login
$ ./rdio-scanner -cmd config-get +out deployment.json
$ ./rdio-scanner -cmd user-add +ident "Dispatch desk" +code 7F2K9Q +systems 10001 +expiration 2026-12-31T00:00:00Z

On Windows the environment is awkward to set inline, so +password <password> is there when you cannot set a variable. Remember that any other process running on that machine can read an argument you pass, so where several people use the machine, keep the password in the environment instead.

The token file is what holds the session, so one sign-in is enough for a whole script. Ask for an action while no session exists and the client prints Not logged in. and exits. When the server refuses an action, the client prints the failure and exits with a non-zero status: a script can test that, and an action aimed at a server that is unreachable is reported as not done rather than passing quietly.

The flags the client mode is not

Three of the flags never contact a server. They act on the deployment on the machine where you type them:

The flags that act on the deployment, not on a running server
FlagWhat it does
-admin_password <password>Stores a new administrator password in the deployment's database, says so in the log, and stops without starting a server. This is the way back from a lost password.
-config_saveWrites the configuration the flags named into the ini file, and stops. See the flags chapter.
-versionPrints the version and stops.

config-set replaces only the sections the file you pass mentions. A file exported from a different deployment carries that deployment's access codes, API keys and downstreams too, so sending one decides who may reach these streams as a listener and where this instance forwards its audio.

19 · TLS and HTTPS

The rdio-scanner server speaks https itself, in two ways: from a certificate you already hold, or from one it asks Let's Encrypt for. Each is a flag, each is remembered in the ini file, and each tells the server which address the https listener should use.

Your own certificate

Give it the PEM certificate, the key that goes with it, and the address to serve on: 

./rdio-scanner -listen :80 -ssl_listen :443 \
    -ssl_cert_file mycert.crt -ssl_key_file mykey.key

Both names are needed: the https listener only comes up when both a certificate and a key are given, and a certificate and key that disagree with each other is one of the causes named later in this chapter. Where your issuing authority signs through an intermediate certificate, paste that intermediate's contents onto the end of the certificate file, keeping the order the authority supplied, because the server expects the chain in a single file.

A certificate from Let's Encrypt

Give it a domain and the certificate, its key, and the renewals are all handled for you: 

./rdio-scanner -listen :80 -ssl_listen :443 -ssl_auto_cert radio.example.org
  • The name has to resolve to this machine. Verification works by contacting the domain from outside, so a DNS record pointing somewhere else, or a machine behind a router with no port forwarding, means the request is not granted.
  • The https port has to be open to the internet. That is the port the certificate is obtained over. The project advises opening 80 and 443, with the domain aimed at the server.
  • A single domain per instance. The name you pass is the only name a certificate is obtained for; asking for a second host name on the same deployment is rejected by the server's own policy.
  • The certificate files sit under the base directory, in an autocert folder next to the database. Treat them as part of the deployment's secrets: an upgrade that discards the base directory discards the certificate too, and another one has to be requested.

In signing up, the server agrees to the issuing authority's terms of service on your behalf. That is what makes the whole thing need no further attention from you: nothing to request, nothing to renew, nothing to restart.

The address the https listener answers on

-ssl_listen expects an address with a port, written the way -listen is. Write the port. Given -ssl_listen on its own, the server has historically listened on 3000 rather than 443, and this release preserves that so running deployments do not move under their owners: type -ssl_listen :443.

On Linux, macOS and FreeBSD, numbers under 1024 call for root. Either run as root, or grant the container the capability it needs to bind a low port, or listen on a high port and let a proxy face the internet for you — setting up a reverse proxy.

Both addresses answer

Turning on TLS leaves the plain address in service, so http and https are answered together and the console shows both addresses when Rdio Scanner starts: 

Rdio Scanner v8.0.0
----------------------------------
server started
main interface at http://radio.example.org
main interface at https://radio.example.org
admin interface at https://radio.example.org/admin

Nothing redirects an http request to https. If only https may be reachable, enforce that at the edge: bind the plain address to the machine itself with -listen 127.0.0.1:3000 and have the proxy do the TLS work, or leave http on a port your firewall does not let through.

When the https listener cannot start

Ask for https and fail to provide it and the process does not continue as an http-only server. The reason is written to the log under the Server subsystem and repeated on the console, and the process then exits the way it exits when interrupted: the plain address stops as well, and the database is closed.

Every cause is ordinary, and the log entry names the address that would not answer:

What stops an https listener, and what it says
CauseWhat you see
The certificate file is missing, unreadable, or not PEMThe server stops at startup, and the log's Server entry carries the reason the listener gave.
The key does not match the certificateSame: the server stops, and the reason is in the log entry.
The port is already takenThe server stops. Find the process holding the port, or name a different one.
The authority cannot reach the domainThe listener starts and the certificate request fails. The failure appears on the console as a TLS error, and the browser is served a certificate the authority did not issue.

A failed TLS handshake and the other complaints an HTTP server makes are written to the console rather than to the log view, because the server gives its listeners a writer instead of a logger. Under a service manager that means you find them in the manager's own record — reading journalctl and the Windows event log.

Apart from the automatic certificate above, the server obtains nothing for you. Supply your own certificate and key, or terminate TLS in a proxy. A deployment naming a flag the server does not have is stopped at the start: the flag set ends the run with an error naming the flag, and nothing listens until the command line is corrected.

20 · Reverse proxies and trusted proxies

Put the server behind a proxy when it shares a machine with other sites, when you want it on the standard ports, or when a proxy rather than the server holds the certificate. Two things have to survive that hop: the long-lived connection a listener holds open, and the client address the server is meant to see. This chapter sets up both.

nginx

What follows is the project's own nginx example, site root included. The server sits in an upstream block on its own port, and one location carries it: the /rdio-scanner/ prefix is stripped off before the request is forwarded. 

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}

upstream rdio-scanner {
    server 127.0.0.1:3000;
}

server {
    listen 80 default_server;
    listen [::]:80 default_server;

    # listen 443 ssl default_server;
    # ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/certs/site.pem;
    # ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/private/site.key;

    server_name _;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
    }

    location /rdio-scanner/ {
        rewrite ^/rdio-scanner/(.*)$ /$1 break;
        proxy_pass http://rdio-scanner;
    }

    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
}

Four directives at the foot of the server block keep the upgrade path open, and they are the whole requirement: talk HTTP/1.1 upstream, pass the Upgrade header through as the client sent it, and set Connection from the map at the top — it resolves to upgrade when the client asked for an upgrade and to close when it did not. Drop any of the four and the result is the same shape of failure: the page loads, the listener connection is refused, and the webapp sits without a single call.

Apache

Apache handles the job through mod_proxy, mod_proxy_http, and mod_proxy_wstunnel; enable all three. The project ships only a stub Apache example — it says what it is for and leaves the rest to you. Here is a working VirtualHost in the shape that stub describes. 

LoadModule proxy_module modules/mod_proxy.so
LoadModule proxy_http_module modules/mod_proxy_http.so
LoadModule proxy_wstunnel_module modules/mod_proxy_wstunnel.so

<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName radio.example.org

    ProxyPreserveHost On
    ProxyPass /rdio-scanner/ http://127.0.0.1:3000/
    ProxyPassReverse /rdio-scanner/ http://127.0.0.1:3000/

    RewriteEngine On
    RewriteCond %{HTTP:Upgrade} websocket [NC]
    RewriteCond %{HTTP:Connection} upgrade [NC]
    RewriteRule ^/rdio-scanner/(.*) ws://127.0.0.1:3000/$1 [P,L]
</VirtualHost>

ProxyPreserveHost On passes the host name the browser asked for, which one deployment answering several names depends on. The rewrite rule catches requests whose headers call for an upgrade and sends them through the websocket tunnel. Leave it out and Apache forwards the upgrade as an ordinary request, which ends in the connection never being made.

What a proxy must not do

Proxy settings that break a deployment
SettingWhat it does to the deployment
Buffering left onThe proxy collects the audio and the call stream instead of passing them, and listeners hear calls arrive in blocks. Turn it off for the location: proxy_buffering off;, ProxyEnableForwarding-style buffering directives, whichever your proxy uses.
A short read timeoutA listener connection is open for as long as the listener is listening. The server bounds one request at 30 seconds and keeps keep-alives on; a proxy that closes an idle connection at 60 seconds drops every listener on the deployment once a minute. Set the read and send timeouts on that location to hours, not minutes.
The upgrade headers droppedThe page loads, the connection is refused, and nothing plays. The four proxy lines above are the requirement, not an optimization.
The host header rewrittenA deployment that answers several names, or a certificate obtained for one name, stops matching what the browser asked for. Forward the host as the browser sent it.

Proxying under a prefix

In both examples the deployment is mounted under /rdio-scanner/, and that prefix is removed before forwarding, so the server handles exactly the paths it expects. Keep two facts in mind before you point listeners at a prefixed deployment:

  • Listeners dial the proxied address, prefix and all: wss://radio.example.org/rdio-scanner/. It is the upgrade header that tells the server whether a request for that address wants a page or a listener, so the proxy cannot be allowed to lose it.
  • A request for /admin gets a redirect that puts the trailing slash on, keeping the administration interface's relative addresses inside its own subtree. Let that redirect through your prefix rewriting unharmed, and make clients keep the prefix when they follow it.

Trusted proxies

Once a proxy stands in front, every connection arrives from the proxy's address, and the server counts its limits per address. Without your help it blames everything on one machine:

  • Three failed logins from one address lock that address out for ten minutes. Name no proxy, and one user's three guesses lock out every person behind it.
  • A listener's access attempts are capped per session and per address, and the log names the address each attempt came from.
  • Every log entry that carries an address — a refused credential, a login, an ingest — carries the address of the machine that forwarded the request.

Tell the server which proxies to believe with -trusted_proxies: a comma-separated list of addresses and CIDR prefixes, such as 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, and ::1. When a connection arrives from a named proxy, the server takes the leftmost usable address out of X-Forwarded-For and treats it as the client's own. The lockout then counts against the machine that guessed, and the log names that machine too. 

listen = :3000
trusted_proxies = 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8

A trusted proxy is a machine you are telling the server to believe, and the header it forwards is written by whoever is on the other side of it. Name the proxy's own address, and nothing broader: a prefix that covers the internet is a list of addresses whose logins, access attempts, and log entries the server will attribute to whoever types the header.

Embedding the listener interface in a page

The project also ships a starter page that frames the listener interface beside your own text: an iframe sized for a phone, a stylesheet that keeps it centred and responsive, and space for whatever instructions your listeners need. You serve the page yourself; its one setting is the deployment's address. 

<iframe src="" width="410" height="608"></iframe>

Host the frame under the same host name the deployment answers on. The browser then treats page and interface as one site, and nothing gets blocked as a third-party connection. Use the same scheme on both sides: when an https page asks for a deployment over http, the browser refuses the request before a connection is ever attempted.

The frame belongs to the listener interface, and that is all it should carry. Never embed the administration interface: it is the machine room, and it is for the people who run it.

21 · Running as a service

A deployment that only runs while someone is logged in is a deployment that is dark at three in the morning. On Linux, Windows, macOS, and FreeBSD the program registers and controls itself as a service, and the same two words do it on every one of them: -service install, then -service start.

The service mode

The -service actions
ActionWhat it does
installRegisters the service with the operating system's service manager, and writes into the service's own configuration the command the manager runs it with.
uninstallRemoves the service from the manager. Your configuration, your database, and your recordings stay where they are.
start, stop, restartAsk the manager to do it. The command is a client of the manager: it asks, reports, and ends.
runThe action the manager starts the service with. It is written into the service configuration at install time; you do not type it.

Talking to the service manager takes the privileges that manager demands: root on Linux, macOS, and FreeBSD, a command prompt run as Administrator on Windows. The service then runs as the account that installed it — normally the most privileged account the machine has — so choose the deployment's folder knowing that account writes in it.

The registration is made under the name rdio-scanner, except on FreeBSD, where the service is rdioscanner because that manager rejects a name containing a hyphen. The display name the managers show is Rdio Scanner, and the description beside it is The perfect software-defined radio companion.

Stopping the service stops the server the same way the keys stop it in a terminal: it is told to stop, it closes its listening addresses, and it closes the database. A control the manager will not perform ends with a non-zero exit status and no comment, which is everything a script needs to know.

A service has no window, so the console lines — the addresses, the ffmpeg notice, a TLS failure — go into the manager's record instead of a terminal. The deployment's own messages are always in the log view, and chapter 14 says how to read them.

Linux

The Linux archive is rdio-scanner-linux-amd64-v<version>.zip, with the 386, ARM, and ARM64 builds named the same way in place of the architecture. Each Linux build carries its own ffmpeg and ffprobe inside the program, compiled for audio for the architecture it runs on, so the host needs nothing installed for recordings to convert. 

$ mkdir rdio-scanner && cd rdio-scanner
$ unzip ~/Downloads/rdio-scanner-linux-amd64-v8.0.0.zip
$ sudo ./rdio-scanner -service install
$ sudo ./rdio-scanner -service start

The install writes a systemd unit at /etc/systemd/system/rdio-scanner.service whose ExecStart runs the program with -service run. From that moment the manager owns the process: 

$ sudo systemctl status rdio-scanner
$ sudo journalctl -u rdio-scanner -f
$ sudo systemctl restart rdio-scanner

The journal holds the console lines. The log view holds the deployment's record, and a journal line the log view does not carry is a line printed before the server had a database to write into.

Then open the port the deployment answers on. With ufw: 

$ sudo ufw allow 3000/tcp

A deployment on 80 and 443 needs those ports open as well, and binding them needs a privileged account, which a service installed as root is. In a container, grant the container the capability to bind them; chapter 4 is the container's own chapter.

Windows

The Windows archive is rdio-scanner-windows-amd64-v<version>.zip, holding the program as rdio-scanner.exe with its ffmpeg and ffprobe built in. Run the install from an elevated command prompt, inside the folder you extracted the archive into: the service is registered with the path it was installed from, so moving that folder later leaves the service pointing at a program that is no longer there. 

C:\rdio-scanner> rdio-scanner.exe -service install
C:\rdio-scanner> rdio-scanner.exe -service start

The Services console shows the registration as Rdio Scanner, with a startup type of manual: set it to Automatic if the deployment should come up with the machine. The manager's own tools address it like any other service — sc query rdio-scanner, net start rdio-scanner, and the same pair with stop.

Windows asks its firewall once per program, so allow rdio-scanner.exe through Windows Defender Firewall on the network the machine lives on, and open the port publicly if listeners arrive from outside the LAN: 

C:\rdio-scanner> netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Rdio Scanner" dir=in action=allow program="C:\rdio-scanner\rdio-scanner.exe" enable=yes

A Windows deployment that answers 80 and 443 through a proxy is the arrangement chapter 20 describes; one that answers them itself needs the certificate in hand first.

macOS

The macOS archives are rdio-scanner-macos-amd64-v<version>.zip for an Intel machine and rdio-scanner-macos-arm64-v<version>.zip for an Apple one. Each carries its own ffmpeg and ffprobe inside the program, compiled for audio for the architecture it runs on, so a Mac needs nothing installed for recordings to convert. Chapter 3 says what is in every archive: the release build compiles the ffmpeg of every release target in a container, the two macOS targets among them, against an Apple SDK its maintainer prepares, and it never starts a program it compiled for a macOS target. What FFMPEG.txt records about those two programs is what a read of their own headers and load commands says — including which ones it read — and a read says how a program was linked, not what it does. A release run on a machine that has not prepared that SDK writes neither macOS archive, names the two it left out, and ends with the exit code that says the release is not the whole release.

On your own Mac you can skip the container and the prepared SDK and let the Mac use its own compiler, linker, and ad-hoc signer: go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg on that Mac compiles them, runs them, and adopts what converts. The two macOS architectures compile each other's ffmpeg binaries, so one Apple Silicon Mac compiles both macOS archives: go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg macos-amd64 produces the Intel binaries there, and Rosetta 2 is what lets that Mac run them. Going the other way, the arm64 binaries compiled on an Intel Mac are run on an Apple Silicon Mac, because an Intel machine will not execute them: the compile leaves the binaries in the target's bundle directory and names the Mac that runs them, and you carry them there yourself. 

% sudo ./rdio-scanner -service install
% sudo ./rdio-scanner -service start

The install writes a launchd property list at /Library/LaunchDaemons/rdio-scanner.plist, registering the daemon under the name rdio-scanner. The manager's own commands work on it from then on: 

% sudo launchctl list | grep rdio
% sudo launchctl stop rdio-scanner

macOS asks you to allow incoming connections the first time the program tries to answer them, and asks again when a new version replaces the old, because the allowance belongs to the exact program you allowed. A deployment whose only listener is a proxy on the same machine needs no allowance for the port the proxy connects to.

FreeBSD

The FreeBSD archive is rdio-scanner-freebsd-amd64-v<version>.zip, and its build carries its own ffmpeg and ffprobe inside the program, compiled for audio for the architecture it runs on, so the host needs nothing installed for recordings to convert. The release build compiles them in a container on the machine that produces the releases, against a FreeBSD sysroot — its headers, libraries, and startup files, copied whole out of the FreeBSD project's own toolchain image, which the build reads and never runs. Nothing FreeBSD is started anywhere in the build, so FFMPEG.txt reports what it read out of the two programs instead: each one is a 64-bit ELF executable of x86-64 machine code, it carries FreeBSD's own operating-system byte, it declares no loader and no dynamic section, and it carries the note its link step wrote about what linked it. The notice also says plainly that such a read describes how a program was linked and what it was linked for, and not what the program does. 

# ./rdio-scanner -service install
# ./rdio-scanner -service start

The install writes a service script at /usr/local/etc/rc.d/rdioscanner, and the system knows the service as rdioscanner — the hyphen is what that manager rejects, which makes FreeBSD the one system whose service name is spelled differently. 

# service rdioscanner status
# service rdioscanner restart

Open the port in the packet filter: one pf rule passing the deployment's port on the external interface, then a reload, is the whole firewall step. Behind a proxy on the same host, the rule is needed only for the address the proxy answers on.

What the service changes about the deployment

  • The base directory is the folder the installed path lives in. The configuration, the database, the recordings, and the migration archive all go there. A folder on a mount that is not mounted at boot gives you a deployment that starts with a fresh database beside the one you meant it to open.
  • The service starts before anyone logs in, as the account that installed it. Keep the base directory out of any user's home folder; a privileged account writing into a home is not what a deployment should ask for. Give the deployment a folder of its own.
  • The time zone is the machine's. A machine set to the wrong zone writes its log and its call history in the wrong hours, and the log view's dates follow it. Fix the machine, not the server.
  • Updating the program is a stop, a replace, and a start. The service points at the path, so replacing the file in place leaves the registration working. Back the folder up first — chapter 23 — and expect the first start after the replace to migrate the database, as chapter 24 describes.

22 · Security hardening

Four things stand between a deployment and whoever finds its port: the administrator's password, the secret that signs its sessions, the keys that let audio in, and the codes that let people listen. The server gives each one a model of its own, and hardening is knowing what each model is, and what leaving it as it shipped costs you.

The credentials and what they are

The four credentials a deployment holds
CredentialWhat it opensWhere it lives
The administrator passwordEverything: the configuration, the log, the access codes, the ingest keys, the password itselfHashed with bcrypt in the database. The cost is -bcrypt_cost, 10 to 14, default 10.
The signing secretThe power to mint administrator sessionsIn the database's options. Generated on a start that found none; a secret found too short to be safe is replaced.
An ingest API keyOne path: posting a call to an upload endpointIn the configuration, listed in the API Keys section.
A listener access codeThe calls its scope covers, for as long as it is valid, up to its limitIn the configuration, listed in the Access section.

The administrator's password is the whole deployment, so start by knowing it is stored only as a bcrypt hash — there is no forgotten-password flow, because nobody can read what is stored, and losing it means working through chapter 15. The signing secret is not a password either: the server makes it on a start that finds none and keeps it in the database's options, and replaces one it considers too short. What it is good for is signing session tokens — a token is not stored anywhere but is a signature the secret makes, valid for seven days, and the server stands behind only the five newest it issued. Change the secret and every session opened before the change is over; that is why the console says so on the start that does it, and why restoring a database from a backup ends the sessions of the deployment you restored over. An ingest key opens exactly one path — posting a call to an upload endpoint — and lives in the configuration, listed in the API Keys section. An access code opens the calls its scope covers, for as long as it is valid and up to its limit. Chapter 9 sets up the last two.

The checklist

The table below is ordered by what each step is worth, earliest first. The first row is not optional: the password the program ships with is published, and while you are still using it the interface says so in its todos banner.

Hardening, in the order it pays
Do thisBecauseChapter
Change the administrator password on the first dayThe shipped password is published, and the interface tells you that you are still using it in the todos banner.15
Raise the bcrypt cost to 12 or more on a machine that can afford the millisecondsThe cost is the price of guessing the password offline. It applies to the next password you store, not to the one already stored.6
Answer over TLS, directly or through a proxyThe login sends a password, and the session token is the credential itself after that. On a network you do not own, plain http hands both to anyone listening.19, 20
Name your proxy in -trusted_proxiesBehind an unnamed proxy, every login arrives from the proxy's address, and the login lockout counts per address: one user's three guesses lock out everyone behind that proxy.20
Give every access code a scope, an expiry, and a limitAn access code with no scope is every call on the deployment. An access code with no expiry is a credential you cannot stop handing out.9
Set the retention daysA deployment that keeps every call and every log entry forever keeps a recording of every transmission it has ever heard, on a disk that fills.13, 14
Keep the base directory readable by the deployment's account and by nobody who mattersThe ini file, the database, the recordings, and the autocert cache are all in it. The database holds the password hash, the secret, the ingest keys, and the access codes.5
Do not put credentials in a command line you type on a shared machineA command-line argument is visible to every other process on the machine. The client reads the password from the environment first for this reason.18
Treat an administrator session token as a credential when you hand it to an assistantThe assistant surface writes when it presents that token: it can add an access code, replace a section, change the password.17
Back up the base directory before you update, and before you migrateThe migration rewrites the database in place.23, 24

The limits the server already runs

These need no configuration because they are the model rather than options, and they are worth knowing before someone runs into one. Notice how every refusal is built: an empty body with a status, so nothing outside the deployment learns which credential was wrong, or how close to the line it was. That is deliberate, and it means the log — chapter 14 — is the only place you can see an attempt at all.

What the server refuses, and how
LimitValueWhat it looks like from outside
Administrator logins per addressThree in a ten-minute windowThe address is refused for the rest of the window. The answer is an empty 401, with no hint of how many attempts are left. The lockout is one warning in the log, under Logins, per window.
Access attemptsFive per session, and five per addressA listener who has used the five is refused, and a listener whose fifth attempt arrives while they are locked out is refused as locked out — a valid code included.
Simultaneous listenersMaxClients, default 200, and per access codeThe connection is refused in silence: the server does not tell the caller why.
Session tokens keptThe last five issuedA sixth login ends the oldest session.
Every refusal—An empty body and a status, on every entry point, so a script never learns which credential it was missing.

What the server does not do

The model has edges, and knowing where they are is knowing which protections are yours to supply:

  • There is one administrator. No second account, no roles, no per-section permissions: whoever holds the password can do everything. The password is therefore the secret of the deployment, and the people who do not need it should not have it.
  • There is no second factor. The password is the credential. TLS, a proxy that the internet cannot reach — chapter 19 and chapter 20 — and a password nobody can guess are the controls.
  • The server keeps no list of allowed addresses. It answers whoever connects; deciding who may reach it is the firewall's job and the proxy's.
  • The upload endpoints are not rate limited. An ingest key is a key: whoever holds it can post calls. Rotate a key you believe is loose, and watch the refusals filed under Uploads and the calls that land under Call ingest.
  • There is no audit record beyond the log. Configuration changes, logins, refusals, lockouts, retention runs, migrations, and the assistant surface's writes are all filed there, by subsystem — and the retention setting prunes it, so a deployment that needs the record keeps its retention days long enough to hold it. Chapter 13 is where that setting lives.

A credential never appears in the log. What is filed there is addresses, subsystems, and outcomes — never a password, a token, an ingest key, or an access code. That is what makes the log view safe to read aloud on a support call, and safe to keep.

23 · Backup and restore

A deployment is a folder and a database, and both of them change while the server runs. Taking a working copy before you touch anything is the cheapest insurance in this guide: an upgrade that goes wrong, a disk that dies, or a configuration mistake you cannot undo all end the same way when the copy exists, and very badly when it does not.

The folder, and what sits in it

The files a deployment writes in its base directory
FileWhat it holdsBack it up
rdio-scanner.dbEverything the deployment knows: the systems, sites, talkgroups, units, groups, tags, options, access codes, ingest keys, downstreams, watched directories, the log, and the recordings themselves — each call's audio is stored in the call's row.Yes. This is the deployment.
rdio-scanner.iniThe flags you saved: the listening address, the database settings, TLS, trusted proxies, the bcrypt cost, the assistant surface.Yes. It is small, and it is the part you typed.
autocert/The certificates obtained from Let's Encrypt and their keys.Yes, or be ready to obtain them again.
The token file the client writesThe session token -cmd logs in with.Not worth backing up. It is a live credential, and it is re-made by logging in.
The program, and the ffmpeg it carriesThe code, and the converters compiled for its target.No. The release archive has them.

That is the whole deployment: the binary and its bundle, a configuration file only if you wrote one, and the database where everything the interface shows actually lives. There is no second state store, and nothing worth keeping sits in the operating system outside the folder, which is why moving a deployment to another machine is a copy rather than a reinstallation.

Recordings are not files to back up separately because they are rows in the database: the audio the server received became MP3 inside it the moment the call ended. A database copy carries the whole recording history with it, which is usually exactly what you want, and the reason the database file is the largest thing in the folder.

Taking the copy

The database is a single file the server holds open, and copying a file while a writer holds it open can produce a copy that is not a database. The safe ritual stops the writer first, and the service manager from chapter 21 makes it one command: 

$ sudo ./rdio-scanner -service stop
$ cp rdio-scanner.db /backup/rdio-scanner-$(date +%F).db
$ cp rdio-scanner.ini /backup/rdio-scanner-$(date +%F).ini

The copy is worth taking whenever the deployment is about to change: before the upgrade of chapter 24, before editing a configuration file you are unsure of, before an administrative action you have never performed, and on the ordinary weekly schedule for everything else. Recordings make the database grow, so a deployment with a long history and a small disk is a deployment that should be watched, and a full disk is a failure that a scheduled copy tells you about early.

A deployment on a server database rather than the default file takes the copy with the database's own tool, using the same settings the server connects with: 

$ mysqldump --single-transaction -h 10.0.0.5 -u rdio -p rdio_scanner > /backup/rdio-scanner-$(date +%F).sql
$ pg_dump -h 10.0.0.5 -U rdio rdio_scanner > /backup/rdio-scanner-$(date +%F).sql

If the purpose of the copy is a subset rather than the whole deployment — one talkgroup's recordings, or the unit list — the Tools screen of chapter 15 exports selected records as a zip with the metadata beside them, which restores into a different deployment than the copy of a whole folder does.

Restoring

Restoring is the same ceremony in reverse. A cold restore stops the server, replaces the file, and starts it again.

  1. Stop the server, so nothing is writing while the file underneath it changes — the service actions of chapter 21, or the terminal shortcut of chapter 5.
  2. Move the current folder aside rather than deleting it, so the failed state is still there if the restore is not the answer you expected.
  3. Put the copy in its place, with the same paths and the same permissions: the database file must be writable by exactly the user the server runs as.
  4. Start the server, check the listener health in the system status of chapter 8, and confirm the recordings you expected are still searchable before declaring the work finished.

A deployment on a server database follows the same order with the database's own tool, and the same settings the server connects with. The dump of Taking the copy is loaded back in the other direction: 

$ mysql -h 10.0.0.5 -u rdio -p rdio_scanner < /backup/rdio-scanner-2026-10-02.sql
$ psql -h 10.0.0.5 -U rdio rdio_scanner < /backup/rdio-scanner-2026-10-02.sql

Everything that was in the copy comes back with it, including the administrator's password and the secret that signs sessions: everyone who was logged in when the copy was taken is logged out, and everyone who was logged in after it has to log in again, because the database now says the earlier sessions are the current ones.

The copy is only a copy until you have restored it once. A restore you have never practiced is a hope, not a plan: try the whole ritual against a throwaway port on a machine you do not mind, and time it, so the first performance is rehearsed rather than improvised.

24 · Upgrading and migrating

Replacing the program with a newer release is four steps. Bringing an older database up to what the new program expects is not a step at all: it is the first start of the new program, doing the work itself, saying so in the log, and archiving anything it cannot carry rather than discarding it.

Take the copy of chapter 23 before updating. The migration rewrites the database where it sits, on that first start, with no second copy and no undo button.

The update

  1. Stop the server. A database the server has open is a database you are about to rewrite underneath a live writer.
  2. Back up the database and the configuration file, as both of them stand right now.
  3. Put the new release in the same folder as the old program. The service of chapter 21 was registered with a path, so replacing the file in place keeps the service working, while moving the folder leaves the service pointing at a program that is no longer there.
  4. Start the server, and read what it says on the console and in the log of chapter 14 before walking away.

A start on a database the new program has already migrated changes nothing and prints nothing: every step of the migration pass first probes whether its work is already done. The pass is safe to run twice, which is what makes a start that follows a failed start an ordinary start rather than a gamble.

What the first start does to an older database

The pass applies the new schema, repairs the few things the new server needs that an old database never had, and then moves the tables in the order their references require: groups, tags, systems, talkgroups, units, options, options-adjacent meta, logs, downstreams, watched directories, calls, ingest keys, and access codes. The order is load-bearing — the talkgroup, unit, directory-watch, and call migrations resolve their references against tables the earlier migrations already filled — and the same pass in a different order would migrate a different database.

The four repairs, and why each one is needed
RepairWhat it gives the database
The log's subsystem columnThe column naming the part of the server that wrote each entry, and the indexes the log search is written against. The entries the old server wrote are filed by what their text says.
The call's recording lengthThe column saying how long each recording lasts. Rows the migration cannot measure are left as never measured, and are filled when the call is played.
The migration archiveThe table left-behind rows are written into, so dropping an old table never destroys a row quietly.
The options key ruleThe duplicates an old MySQL deployment's saves left behind are removed, and the index that refuses duplicates is created over the deduplicated table.

Each old table the pass finds is announced in the log under Database, one notice per table, and a database the new server created itself, or one already migrated, is left exactly as it was with nothing said about it.

A row the pass cannot carry does not stop the pass. The row is archived with the reason written beside it, and the migration goes on. An old table is dropped only once every row in it has been carried or archived, so a table still standing because one row of it could not be read is read again on the next start, and its already-archived rows archive as nothing.

This server also carries rows an old server lost. Older migrations built some of their statements by escaping quotes by hand and left a handful of text columns unescaped, so a single quote in one of them turned that row's insert into a syntax error and the row was gone. Rows like those migrate here, passed to the database as bound parameters instead of stitched into text.

The migration archive

The archive is a table in the deployment's own database, named migrationArchive. Each row records one row the pass read and could not carry: where it came from, its identifier there, the reason it could not move, its contents as JSON, and the moment it was archived. To look at it: 

SELECT "tableName", "rowId", "reason", "archivedAt", "contents"
  FROM "migrationArchive"
 ORDER BY "tableName", "rowId";

Read it after the first start. An empty archive means the migration was complete; rows in it mean history the new schema does not hold, and the reason column says why — a reference that resolved to nothing, or a row the old server had left damaged. What to do about them is your call: re-enter the configuration the archive names, or leave the rows as a record of what was lost.
