The archive is the only copy of the configuration a migration could not carry. The cleaning below drops that table with every row in it, so read the archive and re-enter what it names before you run it. The archive table exists only where a migration had something to put in it: a start creates it only while a legacy table is still standing to be read, so the same SELECT answers an error on a deployment that never archived anything, and one that had legacy tables but archived nothing keeps an empty table until the cleaning below drops it.

Cleaning what the migration left behind

A first start migrates a database and leaves it as it stands: it does not clean one. -vacuum is the one-shot that cleans, and it removes three things a migration leaves behind: the units the migration left damaged, the migrationArchive table with every row in it, and any legacy table the migration left standing because a row of it could not be read. The run clears the records first and compacts the file afterwards, prints one line per removal and the pages the compaction took back, and stops without starting a server. -vacuum_dry_run prints that same listing as what the run would do, and removes nothing.

What a run leaves alone is what a deployment holds on purpose: a unit whose label is one you wrote, a unit with a number range, a unit with no radio number of its own, and every recorded call. Only the rows a migration created are removed, and no recording, system, talkgroup, or other record is touched.

Two things a run takes away have no other copy. The row that made a legacy table stay standing has no copy anywhere — the migration could not read it, so it was never archived, and the run drops that table with it. An option value this release has no option of is gone with the row that held it: the archive keeps it as text, and the configuration the new server reads has no setting to put it in. The clearing runs on every backend the server writes. The compaction is the half that needs a sqlite file: on MariaDB, MySQL, or PostgreSQL the run names the compaction it skipped and stops, and there the database server's own tools do the rewriting.

Coming from the version 5 program

The version 5 server was a different program, and there is no upgrade path from it — the version 6 server replaced it. What carries over is the database, and the way to move it is a copy:

  1. Stop the version 5 server.
  2. Copy its database.sqlite into the new program's folder, renaming the copy to rdio-scanner.db, the name the new server opens by default.
  3. Start the new program. It migrates the copy: version 5 rows a version 6 server had already moved are simply version 6 tables the pass reads, and the rest move by the pass above.
  4. On MySQL or MariaDB, do not copy a file at all: back the database up, and point the new program at the same database with the -db_* flags — host, port, name, user, password, and -db_type naming the dialect — so the pass runs against it in place.

Going back to the version 5 program afterward means restoring the database from before the copy and running the release you came from, because the migration writes into the file you handed it. That is exactly why the move is a copy.

After the first start

  • Every administrator session is ended. A migrating start is a start that checked the signing secret, and a secret made or replaced ends the sessions signed with the old one. Log in again.
  • Read the log under Database. The migration's notices, the rows it archived, and anything the old server left damaged are all there, filed by the pass that made them, and chapter 14 shows the filtering.
  • Check the todos banner. A migration that carried your configuration clears the banner it had; a banner naming something missing afterwards is pointing at configuration the archive holds, not at a bug in the banner.
  • Play a call recorded before the update. It is the shortest single test of the recordings, the talkgroup references, and the audio converter the new build carries.

Two servers on one database is not an update in progress. The migration is a pass that drops the old tables when it finishes, so a second server starting against the same database while it runs is a server reading tables out from under it. Stop the old server before the new one starts, and on a container remember the volume is the folder: one deployment, one volume.

25 · Troubleshooting

When something is wrong, start from what you can see rather than what you suspect. Every symptom with a name below has a place to look first, a log subsystem that records it, and a control that fixes it.

Symptom to place
You seeLook here firstChapter
A talkgroup that used to report is silentThe log, filtered to the subsystem that receives the audio, over the day it went quiet14
Calls arrive and play nothingThe conversion mode, and whether this build carries the converter13, 3
The login is refusedThe log under Logins, and the ten-minute window8, 22
A recorder's upload is refusedThe line the server answered, and the log under Uploads10
The webapp connects and hears nothingThe proxy's upgrade headers, the access code, the listener cap20, 9
A downstream deployment gets nothingThe log under Downstreams, and the answer the other server gave10
The log is full of one messageThe subsystem filter, and the count strip14
The build compiled macOS binaries that do not run on the Mac it compiled them onThe run is the binaries' own execution: the compile leaves the binaries in the target's bundle directory and names the Mac that runs them, and the operator carries them there4, 21
The save bar will not save, or the conflict banner is upWhat the banner says, and the other session that saved8

A talkgroup that used to report has gone silent

  1. Open the log of chapter 14, filtered to the receiving subsystem, for the day it went quiet. A watched directory that stopped finding files says so there, and a recorder posting to the upload endpoints says so the moment its ingest key stops working. The subsystem filter turns this into one question instead of a scroll.
  2. Check whether the recorder is still writing. A recorder that stopped writing sends the server nothing, and the server cannot report a file that never arrived. Look at the recorder's own output before blaming anything downstream.
  3. Ask whether the identifiers changed. A watched directory names a talkgroup from the identifiers in the file name, resolved against the system, and a recorder that changes its talkgroup numbering creates talkgroups you never asked for when auto populate is on — or drops calls when it is off. The log names the system and talkgroup each call resolved to. Chapter 10 explains the resolution.
  4. Check whether the talkgroup is in your scope. An access code scoped to certain systems shows you exactly those systems, and silence on a talkgroup you cannot see is a scope question, not a fault. Chapter 9 is the scope model.
  5. Check the delay settings. A system delay or a talkgroup delay holds a call out of the live stream for exactly that long: it still arrives in the history, just late.

Calls arrive but play nothing

  • The conversion mode. The options of chapter 13 decide what the server does to an incoming recording, and a mode that converts with ffmpeg needs an ffmpeg. Every release build carries one inside the program, compiled for audio only, and a program built with plain go build carries none — a deployment whose converter is missing says so on the console at startup, which is a notice worth reading on every new release. When a deployment you compiled yourself on a Mac plays nothing from the other macOS architecture, the compile leaves the binaries in the target's bundle directory and names the Mac that runs them: look there before suspecting the player.
  • The format the recorder writes. The server converts what it can, and a recorder writing a format the converter refuses produces a call with a database row and no playable audio. Play one on the server's own interface before chasing the network.
  • The recording length. Rows migrated from an older database carry no measured length, so the interface shows the call without a duration. The recording plays; only the number is missing.

The login is refused

  • Three wrong guesses in ten minutes lock the address out, and the refusal is an empty 401 that says nothing about the window. The log under Logins carries one warning per lockout, naming the address. Behind a proxy the address is the proxy's, so name the proxy in -trusted_proxies and the lockout starts counting the machine that guessed — chapter 20 and chapter 22 cover both halves of that.
  • A token that stopped working means a secret that changed. The server keeps the last five tokens it issued, and a start that made or replaced the signing secret ends every session opened before it. The console says it and the log files it.
  • A password you no longer have is changed with the program itself, on the machine it runs on, with -admin_password: it writes the new credential into the deployment's database and stops, without starting a server.

A recorder's upload is refused

The upload endpoints answer in plain text, and the line they answer with is the whole diagnosis:

The answers the upload endpoints give
The recorder was toldWhat it means
Call imported successfully.The call is in the database. If the listener does not show it, the problem is downstream of the ingest: scope, delay, or the connection.
Invalid API key for system <nil> talkgroup <nil>. with 401The key is not in the configuration, or it is scoped to a system and talkgroup the posting does not match. The API Keys section is where the key and its scope are.
A line of text answering 405The recorder posted with a method the endpoint does not take. The log files it, because a recorder doing it is a standing misconfiguration.

A call that arrives and then vanishes is usually the duplicate window: two calls on the same system, talkgroup, and site within half a second count as one call, and the second is dropped. A recorder posting the same transmission twice gets it posted once.

The webapp connects and hears nothing

  1. The proxy. A proxy that drops the upgrade headers answers the page and refuses the live connection, and the page sits quiet. The four proxy lines of chapter 20 are the requirement, not a preference.
  2. The access code. A server with an access list asks every listener for a code, and a listener without one — or with one whose scope does not cover the talkgroup — sees nothing. There are five attempts per session and per address, and the fifth is refused as locked out, a valid code included.
  3. The cap. The MaxClients option caps the connections the server will take, and a connection over the cap is refused in silence. The listener count on the main screen of chapter 8 is the number to look at first.

The log is full of one message

Filter to the subsystem, read the counts strip, and read the message's own words: the messages this server writes name what happened and what the server did about it. A message repeating every hour is a scheduled pass failing; a message repeating on every call is a reference that does not resolve. Retention is the control that keeps the log the size you chose, and the retention pass says what it removed — and says when it could not run.

The interface will not save

The save bar writes the working copy you have been editing. If a conflict banner appeared, another session saved that section while you were editing it: the server holds one saved configuration and will not let a save silently overwrite what it has. Read the section as the server has it now, make your changes in that copy, and save again. Two people editing one section at once is the situation the banner exists for, and it tells you before your work is written over, not after.

26 · Frequently asked questions

The questions administrators actually ask, each answered with the control that does the thing and a pointer to the chapter that operates it.

How do I update from the version 5 program?

There is no upgrade path from it: the version 6 server replaced the version 5 program, and the only thing that carries over is the database. Stop the old server, copy its database.sqlite into the new deployment's folder, rename the copy to rdio-scanner.db, and start the new program; on MySQL or MariaDB, back the database up and point the new program at it with the -db_* flags instead. Chapter 24 walks the path, the migration it triggers, and the archive that holds whatever cannot be carried.

I tried the automatic certificate and get strange errors

The certificate authority verifies a name by reaching back to the machine it was asked about. The port your https listener answers on must be reachable from the internet, the domain must point at this machine, and the name you configured is the only name the server asks for. Chapter 19 is the certificate chapter, and its failure table lists the causes in the order they bite.

The listener page keeps saying a new version is available

The page is a cached copy from before the update. Force a refresh (usually ctrl-shift-r), and if the notice persists, clear the site's stored data in the browser's site settings. It is the browser holding the old page, not the server holding a version notice.

How do I install ffmpeg on Windows?

You do not, not for the deployment. Every release build carries its own ffmpeg and ffprobe inside the program, compiled for audio: the Windows amd64 build, the Linux builds for 386, ARM, ARM64 and amd64, the FreeBSD build, and the two macOS builds all embed the pair this project's build compiles in a container from the source release its manifest pins. A Mac asked for its own pair compiles it with the Mac's toolchain instead, and the container image that does the rest is built from the linux-amd64 bundle. Install ffmpeg on the host only for a program you built yourself with plain go build, which carries none — and read the notice the server prints at startup either way, because it is the program telling you which converter it found. Chapter 3 is the requirements chapter.

Which Mac do I build the macOS archives on?

Either one: the two macOS architectures compile each other's ffmpeg binaries, so one Apple Silicon Mac compiles both macOS archives. go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg there builds the ffmpeg for the machine it stands on, and go run ./cmd/build ffmpeg macos-amd64 compiles the Intel binaries on that same Apple Silicon Mac, where Rosetta 2 is what lets the build run the binaries it just compiled. An arm64 set compiled on an Intel Mac is run on an Apple Silicon Mac the same way; the compile says so and leaves the binaries in the target's bundle directory. The target words are the ones the release matrix spells, and the build also accepts the words Go names a macOS machine by: darwin-amd64 means macos-amd64, and darwin-arm64 means macos-arm64. The published release needs neither Mac: its build compiles both macOS pairs in a container against an Apple SDK its maintainer prepares, and chapter 4 names where that SDK lives and what the run says when it is missing. Chapter 21 covers each platform's service once the archive is running.

How do I put a reverse proxy in front of the server?

The proxy must carry the connection upgrade, because the listener's live connection is one the browser opens through the same address as the page. HTTP/1.1, the Upgrade header, and a Connection header that follows each request are the requirement, and buffering plus short timeouts are the two settings that break an otherwise working deployment. Chapter 20 carries the nginx configuration, the Apache directives, and the trusted-proxy setting a proxy forces you to make.

How do I hear about a new release?

The project's repository publishes the releases, and the repository's watch control tells you when one appears. The release notes and the published change log are the release-by-release history, and each archive carries the program, this guide, and the licence of the ffmpeg it embeds. Chapter 1 keeps the short list of what changed since the last published release.

How do I listen to several deployments from one browser?

Open each one with an id parameter that tells them apart, for example http://localhost:3000/?id=dispatch. The talkgroup selections a listener makes are remembered per identifier; without one, every deployment shares a single remembered selection and the last deployment visited wins.

How do I change the access code a listener entered?

The code lives in the browser's own storage. Append /reset to the address — http://localhost:3000/reset — and the page clears what it stored and returns to the main address. The code itself is issued, scoped, and expired in the Access section described in chapter 9.

Where are the recordings stored?

In the database, in each call's own row. There is no recordings folder to keep in step with the database: the file that is the deployment is the file that holds the audio. Chapter 23 is the backup chapter, and it is short precisely because of this.

Can I give a second person their own administrator login?

No. The deployment has one administrator credential, and it opens everything. People who need to listen get access codes with a scope, an expiry, and a limit; people who need to change the deployment share the administrator password, and the log is where you can see what was changed. Chapter 22 lays out the credential model.

Why did all my administrator sessions end at once?

The signing secret changed. A start that made a secret, replaced one too short to be safe, or opened a database carrying a different secret ends every session signed with the old one, and says so on the console and in the log. Restoring an older database is the same event wearing a different hat. Chapter 22 is the credential chapter.

Can I move a deployment to another machine?

Install the program, copy the base directory, and start it. The configuration file, the database with its recordings, and the autocert folder are the whole deployment. Expect every session to end, and expect the first start against an older database to apply the new schema. Chapter 23 is the restore.

Does this guide cover the scanner webapp and the phone apps?

No. This guide is the server and its administration interface. The guide for the listener hearing calls in the web application is the file user-guide.html, in the repository and in every release archive beside this one, built the same way — a single HTML file carrying its own stylesheet and pictures inside itself. The native applications are the project's own apps. The webapp's behaviour appears here only where a server setting changes it: the access codes, the scope, the listener cap, the delays, and the alert tones are the server's decisions that a listener feels.

My question is not here

Ask it. The project takes questions in the repository's discussions, and the support address is in chapter 27. Before you do, the log view is the deployment telling you what it saw, filtered by subsystem and by text, and it is the quickest way to turn a question into a useful report: what you expected, what the log says, and which subsystem said it.

Five appendices to look things up in rather than read through: every flag with the default it carries, the subsystems the log files itself under, the words this guide uses, the recorders the project knows with how each one gets its audio, and the project's one licence position, stated in full once.

The words the guide uses

The terms the guide keeps, in the shape it keeps them, so that a word in an early chapter and the same word in a late one name the same thing.

Glossary
TermWhat it means in this deployment
Access codeA listener's credential: an ident, a scope of systems and talkgroups, an expiry, and a simultaneous-listener limit.
Administration interfaceThe application at /admin/: the sections, the save bar, the log view, the tools.
API keyA recorder's credential for the upload endpoints, scoped to a system and talkgroup.
Base directoryThe folder the deployment writes in: the ini file, the database, the autocert cache.
CallOne transmission, with its recording, its system, talkgroup, site, unit, and instant.
Conflict bannerThe notice that another session saved the section you are editing.
DirwatchA directory the server watches, with a type that says how its file names are read.
DownstreamAnother deployment this one posts its calls to.
GroupA named collection of talkgroups, carrying an alert tone and LED colours.
IngestThe step that resolves a call's identifiers against the configuration and files it.
ListenerA person, and the connection their browser or application holds open.
MaskA watched directory's template for reading a file's name into a call's identifiers.
Migration archiveThe table holding the rows a migration read and could not carry, with the reason.
Save barThe control that writes a section's working copy to the server.
Scanner webappThe application the server serves at / for listeners. Out of this guide's scope.
ScopeWhat a credential is entitled to see: systems, and the talkgroups within them.
Session tokenThe signature the server makes with its signing secret, presented in the Authorization header.
Signing secretThe value stored in the database that signs administrator sessions. Changing it ends them.
SiteA transmitter location within a system.
SubsystemThe part of the server a log entry names as its writer.
SystemA radio network: the trunked system, the conventional channel, the simulcast, named by its type.
TagA label across systems, carrying an alert tone and LED colours, applied to talkgroups by name.
TalkgroupA channel listeners tune to, identified by the recorder's number within its system.
Todos bannerThe list of what the deployment is still missing, computed from its configuration.
UnitA radio that transmits, identified within its system.
Working copyThe section as you have edited it, before you save it.

The licence, and the two APIs

The server is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3, and that one position covers all of it, including both of the interfaces it answers. The HTTP REST API — every endpoint of chapter 16 — is available under the GPL for any use, a self-hosted deployment's own webapp and a third party's applications alike. The real-time connection a listener holds open, taken over the same address the scanner webapp is served from, is part of the server and not a service standing beside it, so it is under the same terms.

What limits a listener is the deployment's own choice, not the licence. A server configured with access codes asks a listener for one before it shows anything; a server configured without them answers openly. The access code decides what a particular listener may hear; the licence decides what anyone may do with the software itself. The two never do each other's job.

Nothing here needs an agreement with anyone. One self-hosted deployment answers the REST API and the real-time connection alike, and it serves its own webapp, its own native applications, and third-party clients on the same terms.

The ffmpeg the releases carry

Every release archive carries the ffmpeg and ffprobe this project's build produced, and it carries FFMPEG.txt beside them. That file gives the licence terms of the components the binaries embed, states that the pair is compiled for audio only — no video codec, decoder, or encoder, and no network protocol inside it — and lists the codecs the run recorded. For the binaries the release build compiled, the archive also names the container image and digest that compiled them, the source release it compiled, and the configure recipe it used, so the pair can be reproduced from this project's own repository. For binaries the build adopted rather than compiled, it names the host that ran them and the conversions that host performed, because an adopted pair was proved by a run somewhere else. A program you built yourself with plain go build carries no embedded pair at all: it uses the ffmpeg your host's package manager installed, and that package carries its own licence terms.

Getting support

  • Open the log view first. It is the deployment saying what it saw, and it filters by subsystem, level, date, and text. A report that quotes the log gets answered faster than one that remembers it.
  • The project's discussions, on the repository, are where questions and comments belong, and where the good answers turn into the documentation the next release ships.
  • rdio-scanner@saubeo.solutions is the address for support, and for anything that needs a human about the interfaces.
  • The project is funded by its sponsor and by sponsorship. A deployment that earns from the project, or runs it for others, is exactly the deployment the project asks to sponsor it. Starring the repository costs nothing and still helps.

Rdio Scanner is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3. Every interface the server answers — the HTTP REST API and the real-time listener connection alike — is available for all uses under those terms.

This document is written for the server and its administration interface. It carries its own stylesheet and its own pictures, so it opens with nothing beside it and no network.

Happy Rdio Scanning !
